The Finance Manager reconciles bank accounts monthly. The Administrator reviews and signs the reconciliations, and the board treasurer reviews them quarterly.

Individuals' personal funds and property are held in separate accounts, never mixed with agency funds, and managed under IR-05. The Finance Manager performs a monthly reconciliation of individuals' accounts, which is reviewed by a person who does not handle the funds.

The governing body arranges an annual financial review or audit by an independent accountant. The Administrator provides the results to the board and corrects any findings within the time the board sets.

Any suspected misuse of funds or violation of this policy is reported to the Administrator, or to the governing body chair if the Administrator is involved. Retaliation against anyone who reports is prohibited and is grounds for discipline.
Violations of this policy result in corrective action up to removal from the board or termination of employment, and are reported to the appropriate authorities when required.

responsibilities.duty: Approves related-party arrangements, reviews financial statements and arranges the annual independent review.
Collects and reviews disclosures, enforces property and hiring prohibitions and oversees fiscal controls.
Keeps GAAP records, reconciles bank and individual accounts and prepares financial statements.
Disclose conflicts, recuse themselves and report suspected violations.

documentation: Signed Conflict of Interest Disclosure Forms and annual updates
Governing body minutes recording disclosures and recusals
Related-party approvals and quotes
Lease and property ownership verification
Monthly financial statements and bank reconciliations
Annual independent financial review or audit
Reports of suspected violations and resolutions

policies.title: Fundamental Rights and HCBS Settings Requirements
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors, governing body members and all homes
policies.purpose: To make sure every person served by [AGENCY NAME] can exercise the rights guaranteed by Maryland law and lives in a home that meets federal Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) settings requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] protects and promotes the fundamental rights of every individual under Health-General §7-1002, and promotes choice and the exercise of rights in all aspects of daily life. Each home meets the HCBS settings conditions: a lease or equivalent agreement, privacy, lockable bedroom doors, choice of roommates, access to food at any time and to visitors, and full community integration. The home is not gated or isolated and is not located near the agency's other sites in a way that creates an institutional setting. Any modification of a settings condition follows the federal requirements in 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F) and is documented in the person-centered plan. Staff are trained on fundamental rights within 3 months of hire.

definitions.definition: The rights of individuals with developmental disabilities guaranteed under Health-General §7-1002, including dignity, privacy, communication, freedom from abuse, and participation in decisions about their lives.
The federal conditions in 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) for a provider-owned or controlled residential setting that receives Medicaid HCBS funding.
A person who supports the individual, such as a family member, guardian or advocate, in decision making and advocacy.
A planned limit on a settings condition, allowed only when it is based on a specific assessed need and documented in the person-centered plan.

procedures: The Program Director gives each individual and proponent a plain-language rights statement at admission, in a format and language the person understands, and reviews it with them. The individual's signature or other form of acknowledgment is kept in the record.

The statement lists the fundamental rights under Health-General §7-1002 and tells the individual how to file a grievance (see IR-03) and who to contact outside the agency. Before the policy and rights list are finalized, the Administrator confirms the list against the statute and the current community residential rights regulations.
The rights statement is posted in an accessible location in each home, in large print and pictures where useful. It is reviewed with each individual at least annually at the plan meeting.

Staff support each individual to make choices about their daily schedule, meals, personal items, visitors, activities, and how their room looks. Staff document choices offered and made in the daily record (see PC-03).

Each individual has a lease or equivalent residency agreement that gives them the same protections as a tenant under Maryland law (see IR-08). The Administrator confirms the agreement is signed before move-in.
Each bedroom door has a lock the individual controls, and the individual and appropriate staff each have a key. Staff knock and wait for permission before entering unless there is an emergency.
Individuals choose their roommates where a room is shared, and may request a room change. The Program Director records requests and responses. Private bedrooms are provided as required in GOV-08.
Individuals have access to food at any time, with no set meal times or restrictions unless a documented plan modification applies (see HE-04). Staff do not lock the kitchen or pantry.
Individuals receive visitors of their choosing at any time, subject only to the individual's own wishes. The home has no set visiting hours. Staff do not screen visitors unless the individual asks.

The Administrator ensures that each home looks and operates like other homes in the neighborhood, with no gate, barrier, institutional signage or uniforms. Before leasing or buying a home, the Administrator checks its location against the DDA New Site Visit Checklist, including proximity to the agency's other sites.
The Program Director supports individuals to use the community regularly, as described in PC-04.

If a team believes a settings condition may need to be limited, the team follows IR-02. No staff member may limit any right or condition on their own authority. Any limit without an approved modification is treated as a rights violation and reported to the Administrator the same day.

Any modification of a settings condition must be based on a specific assessed need. It is documented in the person-centered plan with the elements required by 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F) and approved through the process in IR-02.

All staff, volunteers and contractors complete training on fundamental rights and the settings requirements within 3 months of hire, and receive refresher training each year. The Training Coordinator records dates and test results in the personnel file (see ST-04).
The Program Director checks each home monthly against a Settings Requirements Checklist (locks, access to food, visitors, privacy, schedule choice) and reports results to the QA Coordinator.

The QA Coordinator includes settings compliance and rights reports in QA data reviews and the standing committee's protection-of-rights review (see GOV-04 and GOV-05). Individuals' own views are gathered through personal contact.

Any staff member who sees or suspects a rights violation reports it to the Program Director immediately. The report is handled under IR-03 or BH-04 and BH-05 as appropriate, and retaliation is prohibited.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every home meets HCBS settings conditions and that policies and training are in place.
Reviews rights with individuals, performs monthly settings checks and responds to rights concerns.
Provides and records rights training within 3 months of hire and annually.
Honor individuals' choices, privacy and access, and report rights concerns.
Reviews policies for the protection of rights.

documentation: Signed rights acknowledgments
Residency agreements and lock/key records
Monthly Settings Requirements Checklists
Choice documentation in daily notes
Rights training records
Person-centered plan modifications (if any)
Settings and rights reports in QA files

policies.title: Rights Restrictions and Due Process
policies.applies_to: All staff, clinical staff, the standing committee, the individual's team and all homes
policies.purpose: To make sure any limit on an individual's rights is rare, justified, time-limited, reviewed by the standing committee, and documented, and that individuals have due process if their services may be ended.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not restrict any individual's rights except through the process in this policy. The standing committee reviews and approves any restriction of a right that is not related to challenging behavior, and sets its time frame. A restriction tied to behavior requires a behavior plan approved by the standing committee. Any modification of an HCBS settings condition must meet the federal elements: a specific assessed need, positive interventions tried, less intrusive methods tried, a description of the condition, regular data collection and review, time limits, informed consent, and assurance of no harm. Individuals have a right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16 when services are to be terminated. Every rights restriction is recorded in the individual plan (IP).

definitions.definition: Any limit on a right, freedom or HCBS settings condition that the individual would otherwise enjoy, such as limits on access to food, visitors, personal funds, or a bedroom door lock.
The committee described in GOV-05 and the QA regulation, with equal numbers of agency staff and non-employees (individuals, proponents or community members).
A restriction used in response to behavior, which must be in an approved behavior plan reviewed under BH-01 and BH-02.
Voluntary written agreement by the individual (or the legally authorized decision maker) after the risks, benefits and alternatives have been explained in an understandable way.

procedures: No staff member may impose a rights restriction on their own. Staff who believe a restriction may be needed report to the Program Director the same day, and the individual's team convenes within 5 business days, or immediately if there is imminent danger.

The team first identifies the specific assessed need behind the proposed restriction, using data and assessment, and documents it. A general concern, staff convenience or house rule is not a valid reason.
The team documents the positive interventions and supports already tried, and the less intrusive methods considered and why each was not enough.
The team writes a description of the exact condition to be limited, how it will be carried out, who will carry it out and in which settings. Descriptions must be narrow in scope.
The team states how data will be collected on the use of the restriction and its effects, who will review the data, and how often. Review is at least monthly, and the review date is set in the plan.
The team sets a time limit and a date for the restriction to end or be re-reviewed by the committee. No restriction is open-ended.

The individual and proponent, or the legally authorized decision maker, receive a plain-language explanation and are asked for informed consent. Consent is written, voluntary and can be withdrawn at any time. Consent is documented as described in IR-06.
The team includes in the plan an assurance that the restriction will cause no harm to the individual, including a description of how health, safety and dignity will be protected.

For a restriction not related to challenging behavior, the Program Director submits the proposal to the standing committee. The committee reviews it, approves it or sends it back, and sets the time frame. A committee member who was involved in the case does not vote.

For a restriction tied to challenging behavior, a behavior plan is developed and submitted to the standing committee for approval before use, and BH-01 through BH-03 apply. Staff do not use a restriction in a behavior plan before committee approval, except as emergency safety measures permitted by BH-02.

After approval, the Program Director updates the IP to include the restriction, the assessed need, consent, data plan, time limit and committee approval date. Staff who work with the individual are trained on the restriction before implementing it, and a copy is kept in the home.

Staff collect restriction data as the plan requires and file it by the end of each shift. The Program Director reviews the data weekly and reports concerns about harm, effectiveness or overuse to the Administrator the same day.

The team reviews the restriction at the intervals set in the plan and before the time limit expires. If the need no longer exists, the restriction is removed within 24 hours. If it is to be continued, the team presents updated data to the committee for renewed approval.

The individual and proponent are told that they can object to any restriction, file a grievance (see IR-03), and ask for the committee to reconsider it. The Program Director assists them and no one is retaliated against.

If the agency proposes to terminate services to an individual, it follows PC-05 and the licensing regulation: written notice to the individual and proponent of the right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16, written approval from the DDA Director, and copies to the regional office and team.

The QA Coordinator keeps a Rights Restriction Register of all active and expired restrictions, with approval and expiration dates. The register is reviewed at every standing committee meeting and in QA data reviews (see GOV-04 and GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews and approves non-behavioral rights restrictions and behavior plans using restrictive techniques, sets time frames and reviews the Register.
Convenes teams, ensures the IP is updated, reviews data and ends restrictions that are no longer needed.
Documents need, alternatives, consent, data plan and time limits.
Implement only approved restrictions, collect data and report concerns.
Maintains the Rights Restriction Register and reports trends.

documentation: Rights restriction proposal and team meeting notes
Individual plan showing restriction, assessed need, alternatives, consent and time limit
Standing committee minutes and approvals
Restriction data and review records
Written informed consent
Rights Restriction Register
Hearing notices and termination approvals (if applicable)

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All individuals served, their proponents and legal decision-makers, and all staff, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give every individual, and where appropriate the individual's proponent, a clear, accessible and safe way to raise a complaint or grievance and have it resolved promptly, without fear of retaliation, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(5) and 10.22.02.10D.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written grievance process that any individual, proponent, family member, staff member or other interested person may use. Each individual and proponent receives enough information, in a format the person understands, to use the process effectively. No individual, proponent or staff member is retaliated against, threatened, or treated differently for filing a grievance, helping someone file one, or contacting an outside agency. Retaliation is a violation of this policy and is subject to discipline up to termination. Individuals may always contact external agencies directly, and the agency never requires use of the internal process first. Grievance trends are reviewed by the Standing Committee as part of the Quality Assurance system. Privacy complaints under HIPAA follow the same process and are also handled under IR-04 (45 CFR 164.530(d)).

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction, oral or written, about services, staff, the home, another resident, a rights restriction, or the agency's decisions, whether or not the person uses the word 'grievance.'
A person, such as a family member, friend or advocate, who supports the individual and helps the individual express preferences and use the grievance process.

Any adverse action, such as loss of a preference or privilege, a change in staff treatment, threats, discipline, or pressure to withdraw a complaint, taken because someone filed or supported a grievance.
Information provided in plain language, large print, pictures or symbols, audio, interpretation or another form that the individual can understand.

procedures: The Program Director designates a Grievance Coordinator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME] if no one else is named) and posts the coordinator's name and [PHONE] in a common area of every licensed site.

At admission (see PC-01), and at least annually at the Individual Plan meeting, the Program Director or designee explains the grievance process to the individual and the proponent, using plain language, pictures, interpretation or other supports suited to the person's communication style.

The individual and proponent receive a written grievance information sheet in an accessible format. Staff document in the record that the information was given and that the person was able to describe, in his or her own way, how to complain.

The grievance information sheet and the posted notice include an external-contact page listing the Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) regional office serving the home ([DDA REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE]), the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) at 410-402-8100 or 877-402-8220, the individual's Coordinator of Community Services, and [ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION AND PHONE]. The page states that the person may call these contacts at any time and that staff will help make the call if asked.

Any staff member who receives a complaint, oral or written, from anyone must accept it, treat it with respect, offer help in writing it down, and give it to the Grievance Coordinator the same day, or the next business day if the coordinator is off duty.

Individuals may file a grievance orally, in writing, through a proponent, through an advocate or by any other means they choose. Staff do not require a particular form. Staff offer to help individuals who need assistance writing or recording the complaint.

The Grievance Coordinator enters the complaint in the Grievance Log within one business day, recording the date, complainant, summary, any rights or health and safety concern, and the person who received it.
The Grievance Coordinator acknowledges the grievance to the individual and the proponent within two business days, in an accessible format, and explains the next steps and expected timeline.

If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, a serious injury, or any other reportable event, the coordinator immediately follows BH-04 and BH-05 and notifies the Program Director. The grievance process does not replace or delay incident reporting.

The Grievance Coordinator, or the Program Director when the complaint concerns the coordinator, reviews the matter, meets with the individual to understand the desired outcome, gathers facts from the people involved, and does not assign the review to anyone who is the subject of the complaint.

Where the matter involves an immediate health, safety or rights concern, the Program Director takes interim protective action right away, which may include changing staff assignments, and documents it.

The agency issues a written response, in an accessible format, within 15 calendar days of receipt. The response states the findings, the action taken or planned, and how the individual can appeal to the Program Director, the Standing Committee or the outside contacts. If more time is needed, the coordinator tells the individual why and gives a revised date.
The coordinator follows up with the individual within 30 days to ask whether the problem has been resolved, and records the individual's own view of the outcome.
The Program Director reviews every grievance for any sign of retaliation. If any is found, the Program Director investigates, corrects it, and applies discipline under ST-07.

Complaints that relate to a rights restriction are also referred to the Standing Committee and handled under IR-02. Complaints that relate to privacy are also forwarded to the Privacy Officer under IR-04.

The Grievance Coordinator presents a summary of grievances, with number, topic, time to resolution and outcome, to the Standing Committee at least quarterly. The committee identifies trends and recommends corrective action, which is carried into the Quality Assurance plan (GOV-04, GOV-05).
New staff learn this policy in orientation (ST-03). All staff, consultants and volunteers review it annually and sign that they understand and will implement it.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, receives annual grievance data, and ensures there is no retaliation.
Ensures the process is explained, posted and followed; takes interim protective action; reviews responses and checks for retaliation.
Logs, acknowledges, investigates and answers grievances on time; reports trends to the Standing Committee.
Accept every complaint, help the individual express it, and pass it on the same day; never discourage or retaliate.
Reviews grievance trends and recommends systemic corrections while maintaining confidentiality.

documentation: Grievance Log
Written grievance or staff-recorded statement of the complaint
Acknowledgment and written response letters in accessible format
Grievance information sheet with external-contact page and record of its delivery to each individual and proponent
Retaliation review note
Standing Committee minutes and trend summaries
Staff annual policy acknowledgment

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, contractors, consultants, volunteers, and Standing Committee members of [AGENCY NAME] who create, access, use or disclose information about individuals served
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of every individual's information as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(4) and Health-General §7-1010, to comply with the HIPAA privacy and security rules for paper and electronic records, and to make sure emergency personnel can promptly get the medical information they need.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps all information about individuals confidential. Information is used and disclosed only as permitted by Maryland law, HIPAA, and the individual's (or legal decision-maker's) authorization. Information is shared internally only on a need-to-know basis. Records are kept at the site where the individual is served and access is controlled there (COMAR 10.22.02.13A). In a medical emergency, the individual's medical information is readily accessible to emergency personnel (COMAR 10.22.02.13C). Electronic records meet the HIPAA privacy and security rules (COMAR 10.22.02.13E). Members of the Standing Committee are bound by the same confidentiality duty (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). The agency designates a Privacy Officer and a Security Officer and follows a written breach response procedure.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health or personal information about an individual, in any form (paper, electronic or oral), that is created or held by the agency.
The person responsible for the privacy policies, the Notice of Privacy Practices, authorizations, complaints and breach response.
The person responsible for administrative, physical and technical safeguards for electronic PHI.

An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its privacy or security, unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the information was compromised.
Using or disclosing only the least amount of information needed to accomplish the purpose.

procedures: The Governing Body designates [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME] as Privacy Officer and [SECURITY OFFICER NAME] as Security Officer, in writing. The same person may hold both roles in a small agency. Their names and [PHONE] are listed in staff materials.

At admission, the Program Director or designee gives each individual and legal decision-maker the Notice of Privacy Practices and explains it in an accessible format. The signed acknowledgment, or a note that the person declined to sign, is filed in the record.

Staff may access an individual's record only when it is necessary to do their job. The Program Director assigns access by role: direct support staff see the plan, health and support information; the delegating nurse sees health information; and administrators see what is needed for billing, quality assurance and oversight.

Records are kept at the site where the individual is served, in a locked cabinet or locked room when no staff are present. Keys or codes are limited to staff authorized by the Program Director, and a key log is kept.

Each individual's chart has a current emergency information sheet (identifying information, emergency contact, physician, diagnosis, allergies, current medications, communication needs and guardian or proponent) in a known and marked location. Staff hand a copy to emergency medical personnel and the hospital, and send it with the individual to any emergency or hospital visit.

Staff disclose information without written authorization only where the Privacy Officer has confirmed it is permitted, such as treatment, payment, health care operations, reports to DDA or OHCQ, abuse and neglect reporting, or emergencies. All other disclosures require a signed authorization from the individual or legal decision-maker that states what is shared, with whom, for what purpose, and until when.

Staff apply the minimum necessary standard to requests. They verify the identity and authority of anyone requesting information, including family members, by checking the authorization or decision-maker status on file, before any information is given.

Staff do not discuss individuals in public, in vehicles, on personal phones, or in the presence of visitors or other residents. They do not post, photograph or record individuals on personal devices or social media, and photos for the agency are taken only with written consent.

Individuals and legal decision-makers may ask to see or copy the record, to request amendments, and to ask for an accounting of disclosures. The Privacy Officer responds within 30 days, or the time required by law, and records the response.

The Security Officer completes and updates, at least annually, a written risk analysis of electronic PHI and applies safeguards as required by 45 CFR 164.308 and 164.312, including unique user IDs, strong passwords, automatic log-off, encryption of laptops and portable media, audit logs, and off-site encrypted backup (see RC-02).

Workstations and mobile devices that hold PHI are kept in non-public areas, are screen-locked when unattended, and are not shared. Lost or stolen devices are reported to the Security Officer immediately.

The agency signs business associate agreements with vendors who handle PHI on its behalf, such as billing or electronic record vendors, and keeps them on file. Consultants and volunteers sign a confidentiality agreement before they have any access.

All staff are trained on this policy at orientation before they work independently (ST-03) and at least annually afterward. Standing Committee members sign a confidentiality statement before each term.

Any staff member who suspects a breach or misdirected disclosure reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately, and no later than the end of the shift. The Privacy Officer starts a documented investigation within one business day.

The Privacy Officer completes a written risk assessment of the incident and, if it is a breach, notifies the affected individual or legal decision-maker in writing without unreasonable delay, and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery. The agency also meets any HHS and other notification duties that apply, and notifies DDA where the event is also a reportable incident (BH-05).
The Privacy Officer takes corrective action, applies the sanctions policy to staff who violate this policy (ST-07), and logs the incident, outcome and corrective action.

The agency does not retaliate against any person who files a privacy complaint or reports a violation. Privacy complaints may be made to the Privacy Officer or through IR-03, and the individual may also complain to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
The Privacy Officer reports a summary of privacy incidents and complaints to the Governing Body and the Standing Committee at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Runs the privacy program, Notice of Privacy Practices, authorizations, access requests, complaints and breach response.
Runs the electronic PHI risk analysis, access controls, backup and technical safeguards.
Controls physical access to records at each site, assigns staff access by role, and ensures staff training.
Protect PHI, use it only as needed, and report suspected breaches immediately.
Keep all information reviewed in committee confidential.

Annual security risk analysis

policies.title: Personal Funds and Property Management
policies.applies_to: All staff and the governing body of [AGENCY NAME] who handle, oversee or have access to the funds or belongings of individuals served
policies.purpose: To protect each individual's money and belongings, ensure funds are used according to the person's needs and preferences, keep them separate from agency funds, and prevent any financial conflict of interest, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(13) and 10.22.02.10A(15).
policies.policy: Funds and property belong to the individual. [AGENCY NAME] maintains a system to ensure that personal funds are used consistent with each person's needs and preferences. Personal funds are always kept separate from agency funds. Individuals have timely access to their funds and may request an accounting at any time. Interest earned on an interest-bearing account accrues to the individual's account. When services end, the agency transfers the person's funds and property to the individual, or to the legal decision-maker, promptly. The agency's governing body and staff have no financial conflict of interest in the individual's money. Because the agency collects room and board from each resident (see IR-08), it must make sure that each person keeps money for personal spending after the charge is paid. For individuals whose only income is Supplemental Security Income (about $994 per month in 2026), this is reviewed before the agreement is signed.

definitions.definition: Money belonging to an individual from any source, including benefits (such as SSI or Social Security), earnings, gifts and allowances, whether held by the individual, the agency or a representative payee.
A person or organization appointed by the Social Security Administration to manage an individual's benefits. If the agency serves as payee, SSA rules apply in addition to this policy.
Clothing, electronics, furniture, jewelry, documents, devices and other items owned by the individual.
Money the individual keeps after room and board and other agreed obligations, for use as he or she chooses.

procedures: At admission and at each Individual Plan review, the Program Director or designee meets with the individual and legal decision-maker to identify income sources, who manages the money, and the individual's own wishes and needs for spending, saving and support. The result is recorded in the Individual Plan.

Where the individual manages his or her own funds, the agency supports the person with budgeting and safekeeping if requested and does not take control of the funds. Where the agency holds funds with written consent or because the plan calls for it, a Personal Funds Agreement is signed by the individual or legal decision-maker.

The agency opens a separate account in the individual's name, or a pooled client-funds account with a separate sub-ledger for each person. The agency never combines personal funds with operating funds, and funds are never used for agency expenses, staffing, program costs or fines.

Each person has an individual ledger that shows the date, amount, source or purpose, balance and the staff member's initials. Receipts are required for each withdrawal. Staff do not borrow from, lend to, sell to or buy from an individual, or take gifts of value.

For cash kept at the home, two staff count the money and sign the ledger at each shift change or at least weekly. The cash is stored in a locked box in a locked location, with separate envelopes for each person.

The individual has timely access to his or her funds. Requests made during business hours are met the same day, and requests made on a weekend or at night are met by the next morning at the latest, unless the individual's plan has a documented, approved limit supported under IR-02. Staff may not decide how an individual spends funds based on staff convenience.

Staff support purchases chosen by the individual, including items for personal enjoyment, and record them. If staff have a concern about a purchase, they discuss it with the individual and the Program Director and do not refuse it unilaterally.

The Program Director or a business office designee who does not handle the cash reconciles each account's ledger, bank statement and cash on hand monthly, signs and dates it, and promptly resolves any difference. The Governing Body or an officer who is independent of the home reviews the reconciliations quarterly.

The individual or legal decision-maker may request an accounting at any time. The agency provides a written accounting within 5 business days, in an accessible format, with staff support to review it.
Interest from an interest-bearing account is credited to the individual's own account and is not retained by the agency. The agency does not charge fees to individual accounts.

If the agency is the representative payee, the Program Director follows SSA rules, keeps benefit funds in a payee account separate from agency funds, uses funds only for the individual's current needs, and files the required accounting reports with SSA.

The agency maintains a personal property inventory for each person, completed within 14 days of admission, updated when items are acquired or removed and reviewed at least every six months with the individual. Valuable items are stored as the individual chooses. If the individual wants an item to be locked up, staff make secure storage available.

Staff report lost, missing or damaged property and any suspected theft to the Program Director the same day. The Program Director investigates, notifies the individual and legal decision-maker, and reports suspected exploitation under BH-04 and BH-05. Replacement or restitution when the agency is responsible is handled under IR-09.

Staff, board members and their immediate family may not have a financial interest in an individual's funds or property, serve as an individual's agent, power of attorney or beneficiary, or be added to the person's accounts, unless the Governing Body has reviewed and documented a conflict-of-interest determination under GOV-10.

When services end for any reason, the Program Director closes out the account, gives the individual and the legal decision-maker a final accounting, and transfers all funds and property within 30 calendar days, or sooner if requested. The transfer is by check or account transfer in the individual's name, and the person or legal decision-maker signs a receipt. If the individual dies, funds are handled according to Maryland law and in coordination with the personal representative, and any benefits that must be returned are returned promptly.

Before a Residency Agreement is signed, the Program Director confirms that the room and board charge leaves the individual with personal spending money. This is documented and revisited when income or the charge changes (IR-08).
Staff learn this policy during orientation (ST-03). The Program Director reviews it with the staff each year, and any finding of misuse is treated as possible exploitation and handled under BH-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy, ensures separation of funds and independent review, and handles conflicts of interest.
Implements the system, supervises ledgers and counts, and ensures timely access and final transfers.
Maintains separate accounts, reconciles monthly and prepares accountings.
Record all transactions, count cash with a second staff member and support the individual's choices.
Direct the use of personal funds and may ask for an accounting at any time.
