Individual ledgers and receipts
Bank statements and monthly reconciliations with signatures
Quarterly independent review
Accountings provided to individuals
Property inventories and loss reports
Representative payee reports to SSA
Final accounting and receipt for transfer at discharge
Conflict-of-interest disclosures

policies.title: Informed Consent, Proponents and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All staff, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all individuals served and their proponents and legal decision-makers
policies.purpose: To make sure that individuals make their own decisions to the greatest extent possible, receive the support they need to do so, and that informed consent is obtained from the right person and recorded before any rights modification, restrictive technique or other significant decision.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] presumes that every adult individual can make his or her own choices and gives support to help the individual understand options and consequences. Where the individual has a legal guardian or other legally authorized decision-maker, the agency works with that person and still involves the individual in every decision. The agency complies with Health-General §5-605, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(12). [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms with agency counsel the current statutory requirements annually, records the confirmation, and revises this policy if the law changes. Informed consent, or the consent of the legal decision-maker where applicable, is documented in the Individual Plan before any rights modification or restrictive technique. A modification of a setting condition under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F) is allowed only with a specific assessed need and documented in the person-centered plan (see IR-02). All staff are trained in supporting individuals and families in making choices and in communication skills.

definitions.definition: Agreement given voluntarily by the person with the authority to decide, after receiving clear information about the nature, purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives of a proposed action, including the option of refusing.
A person who supports the individual, such as a family member, friend or advocate, and helps the individual express preferences. A proponent is not necessarily a legal decision-maker.
A court-appointed guardian, an agent under a valid advance directive or power of attorney, or another person authorized by Maryland law to make a particular decision for the individual.
Giving the individual information, time, communication tools and trusted people so that the person can make and express his or her own decisions.

procedures: At admission (PC-01), the Program Director obtains and files copies of any guardianship order, power of attorney, advance directive or other document showing who has legal authority to decide, and records the scope and limits of that authority. If there is none, the record states that the individual makes his or her own decisions.

The record has a Decision-Maker Identification Page that is current and easy to find. It lists the name and [PHONE] of each proponent and legal decision-maker, the kinds of decisions each may make, and the date the authority was verified. The Program Director reviews it at each Individual Plan meeting and when there is any change.

Staff never assume that a person lacks capacity because of a diagnosis, age or a communication difference. If a staff member has a concern about an individual's ability to understand a particular decision, the staff member tells the Program Director, who arranges an evaluation by the appropriate professional and does not seek guardianship without involving the individual's support team and the DDA Coordinator of Community Services.

Before asking for consent, staff explain the proposal in plain language, using the person's own preferred way to communicate, including pictures, demonstrations, interpreters, communication devices and more time. Staff check understanding by asking the person to say or show what the decision is.

The explanation always covers what is proposed and why, how long it will last, risks and benefits, alternatives (including doing nothing), who will see the information, and the right to refuse or withdraw consent at any time.
Staff offer the individual a chance to talk it over with a proponent, family member, advocate or trusted person, and arrange for that person to be present if the individual wishes.

Where a legal decision-maker has authority, the Program Director or designee gives the same information to that person, obtains consent within that person's authority, and still explains the matter to the individual and records the individual's views, preferences and any objection. The individual's expressed wishes are given real weight and recorded.

Informed consent for any rights modification, restrictive technique, medication used to modify behavior, or behavior plan is obtained before it starts. The consent identifies the specific restriction or technique, the assessed need, the less intrusive methods already tried, the time frame and the data that will be reviewed. It is documented in the Individual Plan as required by PC-02, IR-02 and BH-01 through BH-03.

Any modification of a condition of a provider-controlled residential setting, such as privacy, lockable doors, schedule, access to food or visitors, requires a specific assessed need, positive interventions and supports tried, a time limit, regular review of data, and the individual's informed consent, all documented in the person-centered plan under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F). Staff may not impose a restriction for staff convenience or as a group measure.

Consent is revisited at least annually, whenever the plan or restriction changes, and whenever the individual or decision-maker withdraws or questions it. A restriction ends or is changed promptly if consent is withdrawn and the restriction is not otherwise legally permitted.

Non-emergency medical treatment decisions are made by the individual or the person legally authorized to decide. Staff help the individual prepare for appointments, ask questions and understand results. Staff never sign consent forms on an individual's behalf unless they are legally authorized and the Program Director has approved it in writing.
In an emergency, staff follow HW-04 and call 911 and notify the legal decision-maker, nurse and Program Director as soon as possible. Emergency care is not delayed to obtain consent.

Within three months of hire, all direct support staff complete DDA-approved training on supporting individuals and families in making choices and on communication skills (COMAR 10.22.02.11D). The Program Director records completion in the personnel file (ST-04, ST-06).

Staff recognize and support proponents as partners. Proponents may attend meetings at the individual's invitation, receive information that the individual (or decision-maker) has authorized, and receive information about the grievance process (IR-03).

If staff believe a decision-maker's choice is harmful to the individual or conflicts with the individual's expressed wishes, staff raise it with the Program Director, who consults the DDA Coordinator of Community Services and, if needed, the Standing Committee. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation by a decision-maker is reported under BH-04.
The Program Director reviews each person's consent documentation as part of the annual quality review, and the Standing Committee reviews samples (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies decision-maker authority, ensures informed consent is obtained and recorded, and maintains the Decision-Maker Identification Page.
Confirms the requirements of Health-General §5-605 with counsel each year and updates the policy.
Present information in accessible ways, support choice-making, and never pressure or coerce an individual.
Act in the individual's interests and honor the individual's preferences as far as possible.
Reviews consent for rights restrictions and restrictive techniques.

documentation: Guardianship, power of attorney and advance directive copies
Decision-Maker Identification Page
Signed informed consent forms with explanation notes and the individual's own expressed views
Individual Plan consent entries for restrictions or techniques
Annual legal confirmation regarding Health-General §5-605
Training records for supporting choice and communication skills
Standing Committee review notes

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all individuals served, applicants, families and proponents
policies.purpose: To make sure services are provided without discrimination as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(6), and that individuals and families with limited English proficiency, hearing, vision or communication disabilities can communicate with the agency and take part fully in services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides services without discrimination based on race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, marital status, or any other characteristic protected by law. The agency complies with the Americans with Disabilities Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. The agency provides qualified interpreters, translated materials, accessible formats and assistive communication tools free of charge to individuals and families who need them. The agency does not require an individual or family member to use another resident, staff member or relative as an interpreter, except in an emergency or when the person specifically requests it and the agency has an independent interpreter available. A separate policy to prevent employment discrimination is in ST-08 (COMAR 10.22.02.11E). All staff are trained on communication skills within three months of hire (COMAR 10.22.02.11D).

definitions.definition: A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to communicate effectively about services.
A person who is competent in both languages (including sign language), able to interpret accurately and impartially, and bound by confidentiality.

Items and services that make communication effective for people with disabilities, such as sign language interpreters, large print, braille, captioning, picture boards, speech-generating devices and plain language materials.
A change to policies, practices or procedures needed so that a person with a disability can have equal access, unless it would fundamentally alter the service or cause an undue burden.

procedures: The Governing Body designates a Nondiscrimination Coordinator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME] unless otherwise named) who is responsible for compliance with ADA, Title VI, Section 1557 and Section 504 and who handles discrimination complaints. Name and [PHONE] are posted at each site and in the admission packet.

The agency posts a notice of nondiscrimination and a notice of availability of language assistance and auxiliary aids at each site and on its website, in the languages commonly spoken by individuals in the area. The notice explains how to request help and how to file a complaint with the agency or with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights.

During referral and admission (PC-01), the Program Director asks each individual and family member what language and communication method they prefer and what supports they need for reading, hearing, seeing or speaking. The answers are recorded in the record and in the Individual Plan.

The agency does not deny, delay or limit admission, services or participation on the basis of a protected characteristic. Admission decisions are based on the criteria in PC-01, such as whether the home can safely meet the person's assessed needs and whether the person's choice and needs are compatible with the vacancy. The reason for any denial is documented and reviewed by the Program Director.

When an individual or family member requests an interpreter or auxiliary aid, or staff recognize a need, staff arrange it at no cost to the person and in time to be useful. The agency maintains a current list of interpreter vendors, including a telephone or video service and sign language, with [PHONE], posted in the office at each site.

Staff use a qualified interpreter for consent discussions, Individual Plan meetings, medical and rights discussions, grievance and incident interviews, and discharge planning. They record the interpreter's name or ID, the language and the date in the record. Staff do not rely on minor children or other residents to interpret.

Key documents, including the grievance information, rights information, residency agreement, house rules, evacuation procedures and the Individual Plan, are provided in plain language and in the individual's preferred language or format. The Program Director has them translated or adapted as needed and tests understanding with the person.

Staff support assistive communication. They make sure that communication devices are charged, working, within reach, and programmed with relevant vocabulary, and that staff know how to use them. Staff do not remove or restrict a communication aid except as an assessed, documented rights modification under IR-02.

The agency makes reasonable modifications to its policies and practices when needed for a person with a disability to take part equally, and documents requests and decisions. A request is denied only with the Program Director's and the Nondiscrimination Coordinator's written approval, citing the reason, and the person is told how to appeal.

All individuals, regardless of the home or characteristics, receive the same rights, privacy, dignity, access to community activities and quality of support. Staff do not use derogatory or stereotyped language, treat individuals differently because of a protected characteristic, or deny religious, cultural or dietary practices that the individual chooses.

Staff respect each person's culture, religion, gender identity and expression, and sexual orientation. Support for religious services, cultural events, foods, and personal appearance are incorporated into the Individual Plan at the individual's request (PC-02).

The physical environment is kept accessible in line with each person's needs (HE-01), and information about how to request a modification, including a ramp, grab bars or accessible parking, is given at admission.

Within three months of hire, direct support staff complete DDA-approved training on communication skills and on supporting choice (ST-04). Orientation (ST-03) covers this policy, the interpreter list and how to use it, and how to report discrimination.

Anyone who believes they have been treated unfairly may file a complaint through IR-03 or directly with the Nondiscrimination Coordinator, and the person may also contact OHCQ at 410-402-8100 or 877-402-8220, DDA, or the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights. The agency forbids retaliation. Substantiated discrimination results in corrective action and, for staff, discipline under ST-07.

The Nondiscrimination Coordinator keeps a log of requests for language assistance, auxiliary aids, modifications and discrimination complaints, and presents a summary to the Standing Committee and the Governing Body at least annually (GOV-04, GOV-05).
The Program Director reviews this policy annually, updates the interpreter list and notices, and confirms that translated and accessible materials are current.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the policy and ensures resources for interpreters and accessible formats.
Oversees compliance, handles complaints and modification requests, and keeps the log.
Identifies communication needs at admission, arranges interpreters and formats, and keeps notices posted.
Use communication supports, request interpreters when needed, and treat everyone equally and respectfully.

documentation: Notice of nondiscrimination and language assistance (posted and in the admission packet)
Record of language and communication preferences
Interpreter and auxiliary aid requests, vendor list, and use log
Translated and plain-language materials
Reasonable modification requests and decisions
Discrimination complaint file and log
Training records on communication skills and orientation
Annual summary to the Standing Committee and the Governing Body

policies.title: Residency Agreement, Room and Board and Rent
policies.applies_to: The Program Director, business office and staff of [AGENCY NAME] who admit, bill or support individuals living in a licensed group home, and the individuals and legal decision-makers who sign residency agreements
policies.purpose: To ensure each resident has a written residency agreement that protects housing rights, that room and board is collected separately from Medicaid billing and at an affordable amount, and that the home meets the federal HCBS requirements for provider-owned or controlled residential settings.
policies.policy: Each individual living in a [AGENCY NAME] group home has a lease or other legally enforceable residency agreement that gives protections against eviction comparable to Maryland landlord-tenant law. The Community Pathways Waiver does not pay for room and board, and the agency bills Medicaid only for services authorized in the approved person-centered plan and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland (W5600, per person per day). Room and board is collected from the resident under a written agreement and is kept separate from Medicaid billing and from the resident's personal funds, and the amount must be one the resident can afford while still keeping personal spending money. Consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) and (vi), residents have privacy in their own bedrooms, lockable doors with keys held by the resident and only appropriate staff, a choice of roommates, a private bedroom (no more than four residents per home unless DDA has previously approved otherwise), control over their daily schedule and activities, and access to food at any time and to visitors at any time. Any modification of these conditions requires a specific assessed need documented in the person-centered plan and follows IR-02 and IR-06.

definitions.definition: A written lease or equivalent agreement that gives the resident a legally enforceable right to live in the home, states the rights and responsibilities of both parties, and gives eviction and appeal protections.
The cost of housing and food (including utilities, as set in the agreement) that is not covered by the Medicaid service rate and is paid by or on behalf of the resident.
A residence owned, leased or operated by the service provider, to which the HCBS settings rule's additional requirements apply.
The LTSSMaryland billing code for Community Living – Group Home, billed per person per day, which does not include room and board.

procedures: Before admission, the Program Director gives the individual and legal decision-maker a draft Residency Agreement and explains it in plain language, in an accessible format and with an interpreter if needed (IR-07). The person has at least [NUMBER] days to review the agreement and may bring a proponent or advocate.

The Residency Agreement must include the address and bedroom; the term and renewal; the room and board charge, what it covers, how and when it is paid and who pays it; what happens during absences; house rules that apply to everyone; the resident's rights to privacy, a lockable bedroom door, visitors, food and personal property; and the process for ending the agreement.

The agreement does not include a waiver of any right or a requirement to give up control over personal funds, and it does not make the continuation of housing dependent on accepting a particular service, a particular roommate or a particular provider unless the individual has freely chosen it and it is documented.

The agreement states that the resident may be required to leave only for reasons stated in the agreement, after written notice of the reason and the effective date, and with the opportunity to respond and appeal. These protections must be at least comparable to those under Maryland landlord-tenant law. The Program Director consults counsel when drafting the notice terms and any discharge or eviction follows PC-05.

The agency sets the room and board charge in a written schedule approved by the Governing Body and reviewed annually. The charge is determined for each resident on the same basis, reflects actual costs of housing and food, and is set so that it is affordable to the resident.

Before signing, the business office completes an affordability review with each resident and legal decision-maker. For a resident whose income is Supplemental Security Income only (about $994 per month in 2026), the review confirms that, after room and board and any other agreed amounts, the resident keeps a reasonable amount of personal spending money, set at [AMOUNT] per month. The review is signed by the Program Director and filed.

The agency never uses Medicaid W5600 payments to cover room and board and never bills Medicaid for room and board (Appendix I). Room and board payments are recorded in a separate ledger and receipt system, and are deposited to an agency account, never co-mingled with a resident's personal funds (IR-05).

The agency does not bill for any service that is not authorized in the person's approved person-centered plan and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland, and verifies each month that the days billed match the authorization and each resident's actual days (GOV-06).

The agreement states how absences are treated for room and board, and whether the person has a right to return, including hospital stays and visits home. The Program Director explains this, including any retainer day billing to Medicaid, which the agency documents under GOV-06 and which is never charged twice to the resident.

If room and board changes, the agency gives written notice at least [30] days before the change, explains it in plain language, and revises the affordability review. If the resident's income changes, the review is repeated at the next Individual Plan meeting or on request.

Each resident has a private bedroom, and a room is shared only if the resident chooses it and the choice is recorded in the Individual Plan. The agency does not fill a vacancy or move a roommate without the resident's input, and residents are offered a meeting with prospective roommates before a new person moves in (PC-01).

Each resident's bedroom door must have a lock. The resident has a key and staff access keys are limited to the Program Director and designated staff, who enter only in an emergency or with the resident's permission. Staff knock and wait for a reply before entering.
Residents may decorate and furnish their rooms as they wish, subject only to legal and fire-safety rules (HE-01, HE-02).

Residents decide their own daily schedules, including when they sleep, wake, eat and take part in activities, with only the supports in their plan. Residents have access to food, including the kitchen, snacks and drinks, at any time, and are not required to follow set meal times unless the person chooses them (HE-04). Residents may have visitors at any time of their choosing, as long as the visit does not interfere with another resident's rights.

Any change to these conditions, such as limiting access to food or visitors, is considered a rights restriction. It requires a specific assessed need, documented in the person-centered plan, with less intrusive methods tried, informed consent, a time limit and regular review. See IR-02 and IR-06 and 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi). The restriction is never applied to the whole home as a house rule.

The Program Director checks at each Individual Plan review that the resident's rights under the agreement and the HCBS settings rule are being honored, and records the resident's own view. The Standing Committee reviews restrictions and any complaints about the agreement (GOV-05).
The Governing Body reviews this policy and the room and board schedule annually, and updates it to reflect changes in the Community Pathways Waiver, rates or federal rules.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the Residency Agreement form and the room and board schedule and ensures consistency with the HCBS settings rule.
Explains the agreement, ensures each resident's rights are honored and signs affordability reviews.
Collects and records room and board separately from Medicaid billing and verifies authorized services before billing.
Respect privacy, lockable doors, schedule, food and visitor rights, and report concerns.
Review and sign the agreement, pay the agreed charges, and tell the agency if circumstances change.

documentation: Signed Residency Agreement and addenda
Room and board schedule and the Governing Body's approval
Affordability review for each resident
Separate room and board ledger and receipts
Written notices of changes
Individual Plan documentation of any modification to a setting condition
Monthly billing reconciliation to the LTSSMaryland authorization
Standing Committee review notes

policies.title: Payment for Property Damage
policies.applies_to: All individuals served, proponents, program staff, the Standing Committee and the Program Director
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from improper charges for property damage and to set the narrow conditions under which an individual may be required to pay, as COMAR 10.22.02.10A(11) requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not charge an individual for property damage unless every one of five conditions is documented and met. (1) The individual's behavior plan documents a history of destructive behavior. (2) A behavior plan addresses that behavior. (3) The individual has the ability to pay. (4) The agency's standing committee has approved the payment. (5) The approval has been reported to the DDA regional director. If any one condition is missing, the individual is not charged, and the agency absorbs the cost. Damage that results from agency staff error, poor maintenance, an unsafe environment, or a lack of supports required by the Individual Plan (IP) is never charged to the individual.

definitions.definition: Intentional or destructive damage by an individual to property belonging to the agency, another resident, staff or a third party, beyond ordinary wear and tear.
The agency committee described in GOV-05 that reviews rights, quality and incident matters.
The director of the DDA Regional Office that serves the individual.
A person who supports and advocates for the individual, such as a family member, guardian or other chosen advocate.

procedures: The staff member who discovers damage secures the area, makes sure everyone is safe, and notifies the Program Director the same day.

The Program Director documents what was damaged, the estimated repair or replacement cost, what happened before the damage and who was present, in an incident or property-damage report within one business day.
Staff do not tell the individual that they will have to pay, and do not deduct money from the individual's funds, while the review is pending.

The Program Director checks whether the damage resulted from an unmet support need, an environmental problem, a staffing lapse, or a failure to follow the IP or behavior plan. If so, the matter is closed as an agency cost and the finding is documented.

If the damage appears to be behavior-related, the Program Director reviews the individual's record to confirm that the behavior plan documents a history of destructive behavior and that a behavior plan addresses it (BH-01). If either is missing, no charge is made.

The Program Director consults the individual and the proponent about the damage and about the individual's ability to pay. The Director reviews the individual's income and funds as shown in the personal funds records (IR-05) and records the finding on the Property Damage Review Form.
If the individual cannot pay without being left without money for basic needs, no charge is made.

When all of the first four conditions appear satisfied, the Program Director submits a written request for payment approval to the Standing Committee. The request includes the incident report, the behavior plan references, the cost and the ability-to-pay finding.
The Standing Committee reviews the request at its next meeting, or at a special meeting called within 10 business days, and records its decision and the reasons in the minutes (GOV-05).
The individual and proponent are invited to attend or to submit comments, and communication supports are provided as needed (IR-07).

If the Standing Committee approves, the Program Director reports the approval in writing to the DDA regional director and keeps proof of the report. The individual is not charged until the report has been made.

After the report is made, the Program Director gives the individual and proponent written notice of the amount, the reason, the payment arrangement and the right to file a grievance (IR-03). Any payment is made through the personal funds process in IR-05, with a receipt.
If the Standing Committee denies the request, or any condition is not met, the Program Director records that no charge will be made and closes the matter.
The Program Director reviews each property-damage event for patterns and reports trends to the quality assurance process (GOV-04). Behavior plan teams review the behavior and supports as needed.
The Program Director keeps the entire file for the individual's record retention period (RC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Report damage immediately and never demand payment or deduct funds.
Investigate the damage, verify all five conditions, prepare the request to the Standing Committee, report any approval to the regional director and issue notices.
Decide whether to approve payment and record the reasons.
Make sure no individual is charged without full compliance and that the agency absorbs the cost of any damage not eligible for charge.

documentation: Property-damage report and repair estimates
Property Damage Review Form with the five-condition checklist
Behavior plan excerpts showing the history of destructive behavior and the plan that addresses it
Ability-to-pay finding
Standing Committee minutes and decision
Written report to the DDA regional director
Written notice to the individual and proponent, and any payment receipts

policies.title: Individuals' Household Tasks and Prohibition on Performing Paid Staff Duties
policies.applies_to: All individuals served, direct support staff, supervisors and the Program Director
policies.purpose: To make sure that individuals do only the tasks that COMAR 10.22.02.10A(18)-(19) allow, that their participation is voluntary and documented, and that staff duties stay with paid staff.
policies.policy: No individual may perform the duties of a paid staff person. An individual may perform only (1) tasks shared by the household, (2) tasks documented as an activity in the individual's IP, or (3) tasks paid as part of a training program as required by federal or State law. Chore participation is documented in the IP. Any work that is not shared household work is paid in compliance with the Fair Labor Standards Act (29 USC 201 et seq.) and Maryland wage law. Participation in household tasks reflects the individual's choices and is never used as a condition of services, a reward or a punishment.

definitions.definition: An ordinary task of daily living that all residents of the home commonly share, such as tidying their own bedroom, setting the table or helping with laundry.

A task that the agency is paid or required to perform, or that a staff person would otherwise be hired to do, such as staffing shifts, supervising other individuals, administering medication, deep cleaning of the whole home, or maintaining agency property or vehicles.
A structured, paid or lawfully arranged vocational training experience that complies with federal and State law.

procedures: At each IP development and review (PC-02), the team discusses with the individual which household tasks the individual wants to do and which they do not, and records the tasks as IP activities, including how the individual is supported.
The IP states that participation is the individual's choice, and that the individual may decline or change tasks without any consequence.

The Program Director keeps a household task list for the home that separates (a) tasks shared by all residents, (b) tasks that staff always perform and (c) tasks assigned to an individual as an IP activity.

Staff may not assign an individual any task on the paid staff duty list, including cleaning common areas of the whole home on behalf of staff, caring for or supervising other residents, answering the agency phone or covering a shift.
Staff may not ask an individual to do work for the agency, for staff or for a staff member's family, such as yard work, car washing or errands for staff.
Before any task is added to the IP as an activity, the team confirms that it is for the individual's own benefit, is part of a goal or preference, and is not agency work.

If an individual wants to do work that is not shared household work, the Program Director refers the matter to the team and to the DDA Support Coordinator or Coordinator of Community Services, and the work is arranged as paid employment or a lawful paid training program (PC-04).
The Administrator, with the agency's wage and hour adviser, confirms that any paid arrangement meets FLSA and Maryland wage requirements before work begins (ST-09).
Staff record the individual's participation in chores in the daily notes (PC-03), including whether the individual chose to participate.
Staff who see an individual doing a task that is on the paid staff duty list stop the task, tell the Program Director and document the event.
The Program Director investigates each event, corrects the assignment and retrains staff.
The Program Director reviews the chore list and daily notes at least quarterly and compares them with IP activities. Findings go to the quality assurance process (GOV-04).
Individuals or proponents who believe that an individual is being asked to do staff work may use the grievance process (IR-03) and may also contact the DDA regional office.

responsibilities.duty: Perform all staff duties, offer chores only as documented, honor refusals and document participation.
Maintain the household task list, review IP chore entries, handle complaints, and arrange paid work or training where appropriate.
Ensure FLSA and Maryland wage compliance for any paid arrangement and enforce this policy.
Document each task as an IP activity and respect the individual's choices.

documentation: IP entries describing chore participation and the individual's choices
Home household task list
Daily notes showing participation or refusal
Written arrangements and pay records for any paid work or training program
Quarterly review notes and corrective actions

policies.title: Referral, Admission and Transition In
policies.applies_to: Program Director, Administrator, admissions staff, direct support staff, individuals and proponents
policies.purpose: To make sure that individuals are admitted only through the correct DDA referral and authorization process, that the home can meet their needs, and that a complete record is created at the site at admission.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts referrals through the DDA Regional Office and the individual's Person-Centered Plan (PCP). The agency does not admit an individual until services are authorized in LTSSMaryland. Admission is limited to the number of individuals stated in the agency's Program Service Plan (PSP) and the licensed capacity of the site. No more than four individuals live in a residence unless DDA has previously approved a higher number, and each person has a private bedroom. Vacancies are filled only with DDA authorization. The admission record is created at the site and contains all items required by COMAR 10.22.02.13B.

definitions.definition: The Person-Centered Plan developed by the individual's Support Coordinator, which lists the services authorized.
The State's system for service authorization and billing, including the Detailed Service Authorization.
The number of individuals that the site is licensed to serve.
The planned period during which the individual visits, moves into and adjusts to the home.

procedures: The Program Director receives a referral from the DDA Regional Office or the individual's Support Coordinator. The Regional Offices are: Central Maryland (CMRO) 410-234-8200; Eastern Shore (ESRO) 410-572-5920; Southern Maryland (SMRO) 301-362-5100; Western Maryland (WMRO) 301-791-4670.
The Program Director logs the referral and confirms the referral source, the individual's name, the regional office and the proposed move-in date.

Within [NUMBER OF BUSINESS DAYS] business days the Program Director reviews the referral packet, including the PCP, assessments, health and behavior information, and the individual's preferences about where and with whom to live.

The Program Director checks that there is a vacancy and compares the stated number of individuals in the PSP and the licensed capacity of the site. If the vacancy would exceed either, the referral is declined or sent to DDA for approval first.
The Program Director assesses compatibility with current residents and the ability of the home to meet the individual's needs, including staffing, accessibility, medical and behavioral support needs.

The individual is invited to visit the home, meet staff and residents, and tour the private bedroom. The individual and proponent are told that the individual may decide whether to move in, and communication supports are provided as needed (IR-07).
Current residents are told about the proposed new housemate and their views are considered and documented.

The Program Director confirms in writing with the DDA Regional Office and the Support Coordinator that the vacancy is authorized, and confirms that the service appears in the Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland before the person moves in (GOV-06).
The Administrator reviews how the vacancy will affect the billing rate for the home, since the rate follows the number of people living in the home, and records the review (GOV-06).

Before or on the day of admission, staff create the individual's record at the site containing application identifying information, emergency contact, next of kin, physician, diagnosis, allergies and medication list, plus any other items DDA requires (RC-01).
Before the move-in date, staff obtain the current IP or interim supports plan, medication orders, health care and behavior plan information, and ensure staff are trained on the individual's needs.

The Program Director reviews the residency agreement and room and board charges with the individual and proponent and obtains signatures (IR-08). The agency also gives them the rights, grievance and privacy information (IR-01, IR-03, IR-04).
During the first [NUMBER OF DAYS] days, the Program Director checks in with the individual and proponent, documents how the transition is going and adjusts supports with the team (PC-02).
If the transition is not working, the Program Director convenes the team and the DDA Regional Office and follows PC-05.
The Program Director files a completed admission checklist in the individual's record.

responsibilities.duty: Review referrals, check capacity and compatibility, verify authorization and complete the admission checklist.
Approve admissions within licensed capacity and the PSP, and review billing effects.
Welcome the individual, learn the individual's support needs and contribute to the transition notes.
Participate in the visit, give information and decide whether to move in.

documentation: Referral log and referral packet
Compatibility and capacity review
DDA authorization and LTSSMaryland confirmation
Admission record items under COMAR 10.22.02.13B
Signed residency agreement
Transition notes and admission checklist

policies.title: Person-Centered Planning and the Individual Plan
policies.applies_to: Program Director, direct support staff, the individual, proponents, the Support Coordinator and clinical team members
policies.purpose: To make sure that each individual's supports follow a person-centered Individual Plan (IP) that the individual directs, that the plan is in the record, and that staff are trained to carry it out.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides supports according to each individual's IP, as defined in COMAR 10.22.05, and keeps the current IP in the individual's record at the site. Planning is individual-directed and outcome-oriented, reflects the individual's choices, strengths and goals, and is carried out in the timelines set by COMAR 10.22.05 and DDA. Health and safety needs identified in the IP are met. Staffing levels and patterns follow what the IP determines. Services provided and billed are those in the approved PCP. Staff are trained on individual-directed, outcome-oriented planning within 3 months of hire.

definitions.definition: The plan for services as defined in COMAR 10.22.05, which describes the individual's supports, goals and how the agency will provide them.
The Person-Centered Plan authorized by DDA that lists the services the individual may receive.
A planning process in which the individual leads or guides decisions about their life, with the support of people they choose.
A person who supports and advocates for the individual.

procedures: Before any meeting, the Program Director asks the individual who they want to attend, where and when they want to meet, and what communication supports they need (IR-07).
The Program Director invites the individual, the proponent, the Support Coordinator and any people the individual chooses, and gives a plain-language agenda in advance.
The planning team reviews the PCP, assessments, health and behavior information, daily notes and the individual's preferences, goals and risks.

The team develops or updates the IP using the timelines and content set by COMAR 10.22.05 and DDA requirements, and records measurable outcomes, the supports to be provided, who will provide them and how progress is measured.
The IP identifies health and safety needs, such as seizures, choking risk, medications, mobility, and addresses how the agency meets each one (HW-03).
The IP states the staffing levels and patterns needed to implement the supports, and the Program Director adjusts the staffing plan to match (ST-01).
Any modification of a person's rights or settings conditions is made only through the process in IR-02 and is supported by a specific assessed need documented in the plan.

The individual and proponent receive a copy of the IP in an accessible format, and the individual signs or otherwise indicates agreement. Disagreements are documented and addressed through the grievance process (IR-03).
The Program Director places the current signed IP in the individual's record at the site (RC-01) and removes superseded versions to an archive section.
Within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days of a new or revised IP, the Program Director reviews it with all staff who work with the individual, and staff sign that they have read it.

The Program Director checks that each service the agency provides and bills appears in the approved PCP and Detailed Service Authorization. If a service is not authorized, the Director asks the Support Coordinator and DDA before providing it (GOV-06).
Staff complete DDA-approved training on individual-directed, outcome-oriented planning within 3 months of hire, and the Program Director tracks completion (ST-04).
The Program Director reviews progress on IP outcomes at least [FREQUENCY] and with the team whenever the individual's needs, health or wishes change, and requests a plan revision when needed (PC-03).
The Program Director summarizes progress and plan-related problems for the quality assurance process (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Coordinate planning, file the IP, brief staff, align staffing and services to the IP and PCP.
Read and carry out the IP, document its implementation and report needed changes.
Direct their own planning and decide what is important to them.
Participate in planning and monitor the PCP and IP.
Contribute health and clinical information and review supports.

documentation: Current signed IP in the record
Meeting notices, attendance and notes
Staff read-and-sign sheets
PCP and Detailed Service Authorization comparison
Training records on individual-directed planning
Progress reviews and plan revision requests

policies.title: Implementation of Supports and Daily Documentation
policies.applies_to: Direct support staff, supervisors, Program Director and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that supports in each IP are actually delivered, that implementation is documented in the record, and that every billed day is supported by documentation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] carries out each individual's IP and documents that implementation in the individual's record, as COMAR 10.22.02.13B requires. Staffing patterns follow the IP (COMAR 10.22.08.04A). Daily notes support each day billed under W5600 Community Living – Group Home and each retainer day. Authorized dedicated hours are documented separately from home staffing. The agency bills only services authorized in the approved PCP and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland. The agency keeps hot water at taps used by individuals at or below 110°F unless the IP documents that everyone in the home can regulate temperature safely.

definitions.definition: A dated, signed record by the staff on duty describing the supports provided, the individual's participation and any notable events for that day.
A day billed while an individual is temporarily away from the home, for example in a hospital or on a visit. Up to 18 retainer days per person per year are allowed.
Authorized one-to-one hours provided in addition to the home's regular staffing.
The per-person, per-day billing code for Community Living – Group Home in LTSSMaryland.

procedures: Before each shift, staff review the IP summary, current health alerts, behavior plan information and any changes in the communication log for each person they support.
Staff provide supports as written in the IP, including outcomes, health and safety supports and choices, and follow the posted staffing pattern for the home.

Staff write a daily note for each individual before the end of each shift. The note records the date, the staff name and signature, activities and supports provided, the individual's participation and mood, meals, medication events, health observations, community outings and any incidents.
Daily notes are written in objective, respectful language. They do not include opinions or labels, and they refer to IP outcomes where relevant.

Staff document dedicated one-to-one hours on a separate log that shows the start and end times, the staff member, the authorized service, the activity and the individual's response. These hours are not counted as home staffing.
Staff who find a support that cannot be carried out, such as a missing item or staffing gap, tell the supervisor immediately and document the reason and the alternative offered.

When an individual is away from the home for a hospital stay or other qualifying absence, staff document the dates, the reason and who was informed, and the Program Director decides whether a retainer day may be billed.
The Program Director tracks the number of retainer days used by each person in the year, and does not bill beyond 18 days per person per year.
The Program Director or designee checks each week that daily notes are complete, signed and consistent with the IP, and requests corrections by the next business day.

Before the billing cycle closes each month, billing staff match each W5600 day, retainer day and dedicated hour claimed to the daily notes, logs, the PCP and the LTSSMaryland authorization. A day without supporting documentation is not billed (GOV-06).
Because W5600 billing follows the number of people living in the home, billing staff confirm census each day billed against the vacancy and admission records.

The Maintenance or Program Director checks hot water temperatures at taps used by individuals at least [FREQUENCY], records readings and adjusts the water heater when readings exceed 110°F. A higher temperature is allowed only where the IP documents that every person in the home can regulate temperature safely.
The Program Director reviews implementation gaps, such as missed supports or incomplete notes, with the staff concerned and provides retraining. Trends go to the quality assurance process (GOV-04).
Daily notes and logs are filed in the record at the site (RC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Deliver supports per the IP and complete accurate, timely daily notes and dedicated hours logs.
Review documentation weekly, keep staffing aligned with the IP and track retainer days.
Match every claim to authorization and documentation before submission.
Ensure that undocumented services are not billed and that corrective action is taken.

documentation: Daily notes for each individual
Dedicated hours log
Retainer day tracking log
Staffing patterns and schedules
Monthly billing reconciliation
Hot water temperature log and IP entry where a higher setting is allowed
Documentation review and correction records

policies.title: Community Integration, Dedicated Hours and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: Direct support staff, Program Director, individuals, proponents and Support Coordinators
policies.purpose: To support each individual's full access to the community, including employment, day services and activities of their choosing, and to use dedicated hours and transportation correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals to live, work, shop, worship and take part in the community like other people. Staff are trained on community integration and inclusion within 3 months of hire. Employment and day-service choices are supported as set out in each PCP. The agency does not restrict community access except through the rights-restriction process (IR-02), and any modification of an individual's settings conditions must be supported by a specific assessed need and documented in the person-centered plan. Dedicated one-to-one hours (W1999) may be shared only for people who are retired, transitioning, recovering, or receiving few day-service hours. Under the current waiver text, the limit is fewer than 40 hours of day services, and under pending Amendment #4 fewer than 30 hours; the agency applies the limit in effect at the time. Transportation is included in the daily rate, and the agency uses the most cost-effective mode that meets the individual's needs and choices.

definitions.definition: Full access to the greater community, including opportunities to seek employment, engage in community life, control personal resources and receive services in the community to the same degree as people not receiving Medicaid HCBS.
Authorized one-to-one hours (W1999) billed in 15-minute units.
Dedicated hours used by two or more individuals together in the same activity, permitted only in the circumstances stated in this policy.
Any limit on an individual's rights, including access to the community, handled under IR-02.

procedures: Within 3 months of hire, each staff member completes DDA-approved training on community integration and inclusion, and the Program Director records completion (ST-04).
At IP development and review (PC-02), the team asks each individual about the activities, places, relationships, work and day services they want, and records them as goals with the supports needed.

Staff help each individual use community resources of their choice, such as stores, libraries, faith communities, clubs, recreation and volunteer opportunities, and record outings in daily notes (PC-03).

Employment: The Program Director confirms that each individual's PCP states their employment and day-service choices, helps arrange contact with the Support Coordinator and employment or day providers when asked, and adjusts home schedules and transportation around work and day-service hours.
The individual is never required to work or attend a day program, and the choice is documented in the PCP.

The agency does not limit visitors, outings or community access on the basis of staff convenience or house rules. Any limit proposed because of a safety or health need goes through the IR-02 rights-restriction process, with a specific assessed need documented in the person-centered plan, before it takes effect.
Dedicated hours: The Program Director confirms that the authorization for dedicated hours is in LTSSMaryland before the hours start, and schedules staff only for authorized hours (GOV-06).

Before proposing shared dedicated hours, the Program Director confirms that each person who would share is retired, transitioning, recovering or receiving few day-service hours, using the hours threshold in effect (fewer than 40 hours now, fewer than 30 hours if Amendment #4 is approved), and records the basis.
Individuals who would share hours must agree to do so and be able to take part in an activity they have chosen. The agreement is recorded in the IP.
Staff record dedicated hours on a separate log from home staffing, with start and end times, the activity, who took part and the outcome (PC-03).

Transportation: Staff plan trips using the most cost-effective mode that meets the individual's needs and choices, such as public transit, agency vehicle or a ride program, and do not charge individuals separately for transportation covered by the daily rate (HE-05).

The Program Director reviews each month whether individuals are getting the community, employment and day-service experiences in their plans. The Program Director shares findings with the team and the quality assurance process (GOV-04).
If an individual or proponent believes that community access is being restricted, they may use the grievance process (IR-03).

responsibilities.duty: Support individuals' community participation, document outings and use dedicated hours as authorized.
Confirm authorizations, schedule staffing and transportation, review shared hours eligibility and monitor community integration.
Ensure the agency applies the current dedicated-hours rule and does not restrict access outside IR-02.
Record employment, day-service and community goals and supports.

documentation: Training records on community integration
PCP and IP entries on community, employment and day-service choices
Dedicated hours authorizations and logs
Shared-hours eligibility and agreement records
Outing records in daily notes
Rights restriction documentation where applicable (IR-02)
Monthly community integration reviews

policies.title: Transition, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: Community Living – Group Home (DDA Community Pathways Waiver); all individuals served, the Program Director, the Governing Body, direct support staff, and the individual's team
policies.purpose: To make sure that any move, discharge or termination of services is planned, based on the individual's choices, and carried out only as COMAR 10.22.02 allows. This protects the individual's right to notice, a hearing, continuity of care and the return of personal funds.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not terminate services to an individual except for good cause and with the written approval of the Director of the Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA). Before the proposed termination date, we will give the Director 90 days' written notice. Within that same 90-day period we will give the individual, and the proponent where appropriate, written notice of our intent to terminate and of the individual's right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16. We will copy the DDA regional office and the individual's team on the notice. No individual will be discharged, locked out, or told to leave on the basis of an informal decision or an emergency staffing problem. When an individual chooses to move, or the team plans a transition, we will cooperate fully and make the move orderly and safe. Services are considered terminated after 60 consecutive days of absence unless the Director decides otherwise. When services end for any reason, we will transfer the individual's personal funds to the individual in a timely manner and keep the record for at least 6 years.

definitions.definition: A documented reason that justifies ending services and that the DDA Director agrees to in writing. [AGENCY NAME] does not decide on its own that good cause exists.
The Director of the Developmental Disabilities Administration, who approves or denies licenses and approves terminations of services.
A person who advocates for the individual, such as a family member, guardian or other representative, and who receives notice where appropriate.
The DDA regional office that serves the individual.
The individual, the proponent, the DDA coordinator of community services and the other people who take part in the individual's person-centered planning.
Any consecutive days when the individual is not residing in the home, including hospital stays and family visits.

procedures: The Program Director will treat every request or event that could lead to a move or the end of services (an individual's request, a team recommendation, a hospitalization, a safety concern, a provider-initiated concern) as a transition matter. The Program Director will open a transition file in the individual's record the same day.

If the individual or the proponent asks to move, the Program Director will meet with the individual and the proponent within 5 business days to learn what they want and why. The Program Director will notify the DDA coordinator of community services and ask for a team meeting.

The Program Director will never ask an individual or proponent to leave, and staff will never suggest it, without a good-cause review. Staff who hear of a proposed discharge will report it to the Program Director at once.

If [AGENCY NAME] is considering ending services, the Program Director will first try to resolve the problem. This includes asking the team to review the Individual Plan, adding or changing supports, requesting a behavioral or clinical consultation, and asking the regional office for help. Each step and its result will be documented in the transition file.

If the problem cannot be resolved, the Program Director will prepare a written good-cause request. It will describe the reason, the supports tried, the individual's current needs and a proposed discharge plan, and will be reviewed by the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Governing Body.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will submit the request in writing to the DDA Director. The proposed termination date must be at least 90 days after the date of notice. No termination will take effect without the Director's written approval.

Within the same 90-day period, the Program Director will give the individual, and the proponent where appropriate, written notice of the intent to terminate services. The notice will be in plain language and in the format the individual understands best (see IR-07), and will state the reason, the proposed date and the right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16.

The Program Director will send a copy of the notice to the DDA regional office and to the individual's team. The date and method of every delivery, and who received it, will be recorded in the transition file.

The Program Director will review the notice with the individual in person, answer questions, and make sure the individual understands the right to a hearing and whom to contact. The Program Director will offer the individual an advocate or the proponent for that conversation.

If the individual or proponent requests a hearing, the Program Director will tell [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] the same day. [AGENCY NAME] will not carry out the termination while the hearing process is pending unless the Director directs otherwise in writing. We will cooperate with the hearing process and provide records when requested.

The team, led by the Program Director, will develop a written transition plan with the individual and the proponent. The plan will cover the new setting, a visit before the move, the individual's belongings, communication aids, health needs, medications, behavior supports, school or day program, and staff who will go with the person for the move if that is needed.

Before the move, the nurse or designated staff will prepare a current medication list, the MAR, allergy information, physician information, the current Individual Plan, and emergency contacts. These will be given to the receiving provider with the individual's or proponent's written consent (see IR-04).

The Program Director will make sure the individual's personal funds, valuables and property are inventoried with the individual (or proponent). Personal funds will be accounted for and transferred to the individual in a timely manner, with a receipt signed by the person receiving them (see IR-05).

The Program Director will monitor consecutive days of absence for each individual. If an individual is away for 30 consecutive days, the Program Director will notify the regional office and the team to discuss the individual's plans. At 60 consecutive days, the Program Director will ask the Director whether the services will be treated as terminated or whether the Director decides otherwise.

On the day of discharge, the Program Director will complete a discharge summary documenting the date, the reason, where the individual went, who accompanied the person, belongings and funds returned, and records and medications sent.

After discharge, the Program Director will follow up with the individual, the proponent and the receiving provider within 14 days to confirm the transition went well, and will document any concerns raised.

The Program Director will close the record and store it in a secure place, organized for easy access, for at least 6 years after services end (see RC-01 and RC-02). The record will be kept even if the individual later dies.

The Governing Body or its designated committee will review each termination, discharge and transition each quarter for patterns, and the results will be reported in the quality assurance plan (see GOV-04).

policies.title: Medication Administration and Medication Technician Certification
policies.applies_to: All staff who give medication or treatments, the Program Director, the Delegating Nurse, and every individual who receives medication in the home
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual receives medication safely, accurately and with dignity. Medication will be given only by people who are trained and certified as the Maryland Board of Nursing and the DDA require, and under the oversight of the Delegating Nurse.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will administer all medication according to the DDA's curriculum on medication training. Unlicensed staff who give medication or treatments must be certified by the Maryland Board of Nursing as Medication Technicians and must work under RN delegation. Medication administration training will be completed before any staff person works independently. Oral solid medication will be supplied in unit-dose packages unless the individual's Individual Plan (IP) says otherwise. Medication for an individual who will be away from the home will be sent in a separate, easily identified pharmaceutical package. We will ask the pharmacy for computer-generated medication administration records (MARs), treatment administration records (TARs) and physician order forms. Each individual's record will contain a current medication list and allergy list.

definitions.definition: An unlicensed staff person certified by the Maryland Board of Nursing to give medications and treatments under delegation by a registered nurse.
The registered nurse who delegates medication and treatment tasks to unlicensed staff and oversees them (see HW-02).
Medication Administration Record and Treatment Administration Record, which document each dose or treatment given, refused or held.
Medication packaged by the pharmacy in individually sealed single doses.
Any dose given or not given in a way that does not match the prescriber's order, including wrong person, drug, dose, time or route, an omitted dose or an unauthorized dose.

procedures: Before an unlicensed staff person works independently, the Program Director will confirm that the person has completed the medication administration training required by the DDA curriculum. The Program Director will not assign any staff person to independent duties until the training is documented.

Before any staff person gives medication, the Program Director will verify and copy the person's current Maryland Board of Nursing Medication Technician certification. The Program Director will check the certification expiration date monthly and remove from medication duties anyone whose certification lapses.

The Delegating Nurse will delegate in writing, for each individual and each task, the medications and treatments the Medication Technician may give. Staff will not give a medication or treatment that has not been delegated to them (see HW-02).

Staff will request that the pharmacy send medications in unit-dose packages for oral solids unless the IP says otherwise. If a different package is used, the reason and IP reference will be noted in the record.

Staff will ask the pharmacy for computer-generated MARs, TARs and physician order forms for each individual. Staff will not hand-write a new MAR unless the pharmacy cannot supply one, and any hand-written entry will be reviewed by the Delegating Nurse within one business day.

When medication is received, a trained staff person will check the label against the physician order and the MAR for the individual's name, drug, dose, route, time and allergies. Any difference will be reported to the pharmacy and the Delegating Nurse before the dose is given.

Staff will store medications in a locked, clean and properly cooled or room-temperature area according to the label. Only staff who have been delegated medication duties will hold keys. Individuals who self-administer under their IP will store their medication according to their IP.

Before each administration, the Medication Technician will wash hands, confirm the individual's identity, check the MAR and label, explain what is being given, offer the medication with water or a food suitable for the person, and watch the person take it.

The Medication Technician will document on the MAR immediately after the individual takes the dose. A dose will never be documented ahead of time. If an individual refuses, or a dose is held or missed, the staff person will write the reason on the MAR and notify the Delegating Nurse the same day.

When an individual will be away from the home (for family visits, trips or overnight stays), the staff person will prepare the medication for the absence in a separate, easily identified pharmaceutical package labeled with the individual's name, drug, dose and times. A staff person will review the instructions with the person receiving the medication and record what was sent and when it was returned.

Staff will keep a current medication list and allergy list in each individual's record and update them at once whenever a physician or nurse practitioner orders a change. The Delegating Nurse will review the lists at least quarterly and after every hospital stay.

When a medication error occurs, staff will make sure the individual is safe, call the prescriber or Delegating Nurse for instructions, follow those instructions, and complete the incident report required by DDA procedures (see BH-05). Staff will tell the Program Director the same day.

The Delegating Nurse and Program Director will review each medication error for cause and corrective action, and will report the results to the standing committee as part of incident review (see GOV-05).

Medications that are discontinued, expired or refused will be separated from current medications, locked, and disposed of according to the Delegating Nurse's instructions and a documented count with two staff signatures.

The Delegating Nurse will observe each Medication Technician giving medication as part of regular oversight and document it. The Program Director will review MARs and TARs monthly for gaps, and the results will be included in the quality assurance review (see GOV-04).
Staff will take the MAR, medication list and allergy list when an individual goes for emergency care, so the information is available to emergency personnel (see HW-04).

policies.title: Delegating Nurse Oversight and Health Care Coordination
policies.applies_to: The Delegating Nurse, Program Director, Medication Technicians and direct support staff who perform delegated nursing tasks, and the individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure that nursing tasks performed by unlicensed staff are delegated, supervised and documented by a registered nurse in line with COMAR 10.27.11, and that each individual's health care is coordinated among the individual, the team, physicians and the nurse.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will comply with COMAR 10.27.11, Delegation of Nursing Functions. A registered nurse will delegate nursing tasks to unlicensed staff, and no unlicensed staff person will perform a nursing task that has not been delegated. Nursing support services are included within Community Living – Group Home according to each individual's assessed need. If an individual's health changes or the person is discharged from a hospital, we will ask the DDA Regional Office to authorize additional standalone nursing hours when the person needs them. Each individual's record will contain the person's physician, diagnosis and medication list. Before this policy is finalized for use, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Delegating Nurse will read COMAR 10.27.11 and make sure the procedures below match it.

definitions.definition: A registered nurse's transfer of a nursing task to a trained, competent unlicensed person while the nurse remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for supervision.
The registered nurse who assesses the individual and the staff person, decides which tasks may be delegated, teaches and supervises.
Nursing services that are included in the Community Living – Group Home service based on assessed need.
Arranging and following up on medical appointments, orders, test results and communication among the individual, physicians, the team and the staff.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will contract with or employ a registered nurse who holds a current Maryland license and who agrees in writing to act as Delegating Nurse. The Program Director will keep a copy of the license on file and verify it annually.

Before any nursing task is delegated, the Delegating Nurse will assess the individual's health needs and the task to be delegated, and will decide whether delegation is appropriate under COMAR 10.27.11. The assessment will be documented.
The Delegating Nurse will assess the staff person's competence for each task, teach the task, watch the staff person perform it, and document the results before the person performs it alone.

The Delegating Nurse will issue written delegation instructions for each task and each individual. They will state the task, the individual, the instructions for doing it, what to watch for, and when to call the nurse or 911.

Staff will perform only the delegated tasks. If a staff person is unsure, feels the task is unsafe, or the individual's condition has changed, the staff person will stop and call the Delegating Nurse before continuing.

The Delegating Nurse will provide ongoing supervision and will be reachable by phone for questions at the number posted in the home, [PHONE]. The Program Director will make sure the after-hours contact is posted for every shift.

The Delegating Nurse will review the delegation for each staff person and individual at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., every 90 days] and any time the individual's condition, orders or the staff person's performance changes. Delegation will be withdrawn if the staff person is not competent.
The Program Director will make sure each individual's record contains the person's physician, diagnosis and current medication list, and that the Delegating Nurse reviews them at least quarterly.

Staff will schedule routine medical, dental and specialty appointments as the individual and team choose and as the IP provides. Staff will take current information to each appointment and bring back written orders and instructions.

After each appointment or hospitalization, the Program Director will give the new orders and instructions to the Delegating Nurse within one business day. The nurse will update the medication list, delegation instructions and health care information, and tell the team.

When an individual's health changes or the person returns from the hospital, the Delegating Nurse will assess whether additional nursing support is needed. If it is, the Program Director will ask the DDA Regional Office, through the coordinator of community services, to authorize additional standalone nursing hours.
The Delegating Nurse will teach direct support staff about each individual's health needs, including diagnoses, warning signs and what to do (see HW-03).

The Delegating Nurse will report to the Program Director at least quarterly on delegation, health trends, medication errors, and nursing needs. The Program Director will include the report in the quality assurance review (see GOV-04).
The Program Director will keep delegation records in a place that is easy for the nurse and surveyors to review and will update them when staff leave or change tasks.

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Program Director, the Delegating Nurse and the individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure that each individual's health and safety needs identified in the IP are met every day, that staff are trained to recognize and respond to seizures and choking and age-related changes, and that health information is recorded accurately.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will meet the health and safety needs that are identified in each individual's Individual Plan (IP). Staff will complete DDA-approved seizure disorders training, and aging-process training, before they work independently, and First Aid/CPR training within 3 months of hire. The waiver standard requires CPR/First Aid with an in-person skills check, and we will meet it. Each individual's diagnoses and allergies will be recorded in the record. Choking-risk protocols are individualized and belong in the IP. COMAR 10.22.02 does not set a specific choking protocol, so [AGENCY NAME] will rely on the IP, the physician's and clinician's orders and the Delegating Nurse's instructions.

definitions.definition: Regular observation and recording of an individual's health, such as vital signs, weight, eating and drinking, sleep, behavior changes and any condition listed in the IP.
Written instructions, based on the physician's orders, telling staff how to respond to a person's seizure, when to give any ordered rescue medication, and when to call 911.
Written instructions in the IP, based on assessment by a qualified clinician, that tell staff how to prepare food and liquids, position the person, supervise meals and respond to choking.
Work done without another trained staff person present and supervising.

procedures: At admission and at each IP review, the Program Director and Delegating Nurse will read the IP and identify each health and safety need, including seizure disorders, swallowing and choking risks, aging-related needs, allergies and chronic conditions. They will list the supports required and who provides them.

Before any staff person works independently, the Program Director will confirm that the staff person has completed DDA-approved seizure disorders training and aging-process training, and will record the dates.

Within 3 months of hire, each staff person will complete First Aid and CPR through the American Red Cross or an equivalent program, including an in-person skills check. The Program Director will track expirations and schedule renewals before they lapse (see ST-04).

The Delegating Nurse will prepare a one-page health summary for each individual listing diagnoses, allergies, medications, seizure and choking protocols, and emergency contacts, and will keep it where all staff on duty can find it, while protecting privacy (see IR-04).
Before staff work alone with an individual, the Delegating Nurse or Program Director will go over the individual's health summary and protocols with them and document it.

For individuals with seizures, staff will follow the seizure protocol in the IP and the physician's orders. During a seizure staff will stay with the person, keep the person safe, note the time, and call 911 as the protocol directs.

After each seizure, staff will record the date, time, length, what was observed, any rescue medication given, the person's recovery and who was notified, and will tell the Delegating Nurse the same day.

For individuals at risk of choking, staff will follow the protocol in the IP, including food textures and liquid consistency, positioning, pace, supervision during meals and the response to choking (see HE-04 for modified diets). Staff will not change a diet texture unless the IP or a clinician's order says to.

If staff observe a new swallowing problem, coughing during meals, weight loss or other warning signs, they will notify the Delegating Nurse the same day so the individual can be referred for evaluation. Staff will then follow any interim instructions.

Staff will watch for changes that come with aging, such as changes in mobility, hearing, vision, memory, appetite or sleep, and will report them to the Delegating Nurse and the team so the IP can be updated.
Staff will document daily health observations required by the IP in the individual's daily notes (see PC-03), and will record any health or safety concerns as soon as they are noticed.

The Program Director will make sure each record contains current diagnoses and allergies and that the allergy information is also on the MAR and the emergency information sheet. The Delegating Nurse will verify them at least quarterly.

Any seizure, choking event or injury that meets the definition of a reportable incident will be reported and investigated under DDA procedures (see BH-05). Staff will call 911 first in any emergency (see HW-04).
The Program Director will review health monitoring and seizure and choking events quarterly with the Delegating Nurse, and will include trends in the quality assurance review (see GOV-04).

Prepares health summaries and protocols, trains staff on them, reviews events and follows up on referrals.
