policies.title: Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, the Delegating Nurse, and the individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure staff recognize a change in an individual's condition, get emergency care without delay, give emergency personnel the information they need, and notify the right people afterward.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will respond promptly to any change in an individual's condition and to any medical emergency. On notification of a medical emergency, we will make the individual's medical information readily accessible to emergency personnel. Emergency contact, next of kin and physician information will be in each individual's record. Incidents involving life-threatening conditions will be reported and investigated under DDA procedures. Our quality assurance system will respond promptly and appropriately when an individual's health or safety is at risk. Staff may disclose protected health information to emergency personnel and others as needed to prevent a serious and imminent threat to an individual's health or safety, consistent with 45 CFR 164.512(j) and the agency's privacy policy.

definitions.definition: Any new or worsening sign or symptom, change in behavior, function, appetite, alertness or mood, injury, or other difference from the individual's usual baseline.

A condition that may be life-threatening or cause serious harm if care is delayed, such as unresponsiveness, trouble breathing, chest pain, severe bleeding, a prolonged seizure, choking, or suspected stroke.
A one-to-two page summary of identification, diagnoses, allergies, medications, physician, emergency contacts, proponent and communication needs that goes with the individual to emergency care.
A family member, guardian or other advocate of the individual.

procedures: In any life-threatening emergency, the staff person on duty will call 911 first, start first aid or CPR if trained and needed, and stay with the individual until emergency responders take over. Staff will not delay calling 911 to reach a supervisor or nurse.

Staff will send for or take the individual's emergency information sheet, current medication list and MAR, allergy list, insurance information and the IP's health summary, and will give them to emergency personnel on arrival or take them to the hospital.

A staff person will go with the individual to the hospital or emergency care when possible, or arrange for another staff person to go, while meeting supervision needs for the other individuals at home. The staff person will stay until a family member, proponent or relief staff takes over, as the Program Director directs.

While at the hospital, staff will give emergency staff accurate information about the individual's baseline, communication methods, seizure and choking protocols, behavior supports and consent arrangements. Staff will disclose only what is needed to treat the individual or prevent a serious threat.

For a change in condition that is not an emergency, the staff person will record what was seen, check the individual's vital signs as delegated, and call the Delegating Nurse the same shift to receive instructions. The staff person will call the individual's physician if told to.

Staff will follow the nurse's or physician's instructions, observe the individual more closely, document each check in the daily notes, and report again if the condition gets worse or does not improve. If in doubt, staff will call 911.

The staff person will notify the Program Director as soon as the situation is safe, and no later than the end of the shift for non-emergencies. The Program Director will notify the Delegating Nurse if the nurse has not already been told.

The Program Director will notify the individual's proponent or family and the next of kin, and the DDA coordinator of community services, as soon as practical, and in accordance with the individual's wishes and any consent on file. The notification, the time and the person reached will be documented.

The Program Director will determine whether the event meets the definition of a reportable incident, including life-threatening conditions, and, if so, will report it to the DDA and OHCQ and start an investigation under DDA procedures (see BH-05 and RC-03). The Program Director will not delay care to complete a report.

After a hospitalization or emergency visit, the Program Director will obtain discharge instructions, new orders and medication changes, and give them to the Delegating Nurse within one business day. The nurse will update the medication list, delegation and health summary (see HW-01 and HW-02).

The Program Director will arrange follow-up appointments and ask the team to review the IP if the individual's needs have changed, including a request for additional nursing hours if needed (see HW-02).

The Program Director will confirm that each individual's record contains emergency contact, next of kin and physician information, and will check and update it at least every 6 months and whenever it changes.

The quality assurance system will review each emergency and change-of-condition event to check that staff responded promptly and appropriately and to find any risk to the individual's health or safety. The Program Director will take corrective action right away if an individual is at risk and will report to the standing committee (see GOV-04 and GOV-05).
All staff will be trained on this policy at orientation and at least annually, and emergency information sheets will be kept where staff on every shift can find them quickly.

responsibilities.duty: Call 911 in an emergency, give first aid or CPR, take medical information, notify the nurse and Program Director, and document.
Notifies family, proponent and the DDA coordinator, decides whether the event is reportable, keeps emergency information current and arranges follow-up.
Gives direction on changes in condition, reviews hospital discharge orders and updates health information.

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the Delegating Nurse, the Governing Body and the standing committee
policies.purpose: To make sure that when an individual dies, the death is handled with dignity and respect, reported under DDA procedures, the family and proponent are told compassionately, the other individuals in the home are supported, and the person's funds, property and records are handled correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will report the death of any individual under DDA procedures on reportable incidents. The reporting level and deadline will be those in the DDA's current policy, and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will confirm them each year: [CURRENT DDA DEATH REPORTING LEVEL AND DEADLINE - confirm against DDA's current reportable incident policy]. We will notify the family or proponent and the DDA regional office. Our standing committee will review the death as part of its review of all incidents. We will return the individual's personal funds and property in a timely manner. We will keep the individual's record for at least 6 years after the person dies. The privacy of a deceased individual's health information continues to be protected for as long as 45 CFR 164.502(f) provides, and we will release information only as the law and our privacy policy permit.

definitions.definition: An event, including a death, that must be reported to the DDA and the licensing agent under DDA procedures.
A family member, guardian or other advocate of the individual.
The person with legal authority to act for the deceased individual or the estate, who may receive the person's funds, property and records as the law allows.
A structured review of the circumstances of a death to look for lessons for the individual's remaining peers and for the program (see GOV-04).

procedures: If an individual is found without a pulse or not breathing, staff will call 911 at once and start CPR unless there is a valid do-not-resuscitate or similar order, following HW-04. Staff will stay with the individual and follow the instructions of emergency responders.
The staff person will notify the Program Director immediately by phone, day or night. The Program Director will notify [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Delegating Nurse without delay.

Staff will not disturb the area more than is needed for emergency care. They will keep the individual's medications, MAR and records, and will leave the room as directed by emergency responders or law enforcement. They will not discard anything related to the death.

The Program Director will make sure that a staff person who knows the individual stays with the person and with the family until the family or proponent arrives, as far as the family and the situation allow.

The Program Director or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] will personally notify the proponent, family or next of kin as soon as possible, by phone and in a caring way, using the emergency contact information in the record. The notification, the time and the name of the person told will be documented.

The Program Director will notify the DDA regional office and the DDA coordinator of community services as soon as possible. The Program Director will file the report under DDA procedures on reportable incidents by the deadline for the applicable reporting level, which [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirmed as listed in this policy, and will keep proof of submission (see BH-05 and RC-03).

The Program Director will start an internal review immediately. The review will gather the daily notes, MARs, health records, incident reports and staff statements, and will preserve them. The Program Director will cooperate fully with the medical examiner, law enforcement, OHCQ and any DDA investigation.

Staff will follow the family's wishes and the individual's known wishes about religious and cultural practices, funeral arrangements and any advance directive on file. They will treat the individual's body with dignity until the funeral home or medical examiner takes it.

The Program Director will arrange support for the other individuals in the home, telling each one about the death in a way that suits the person's understanding, making counseling or grief support available and letting individuals take part in remembrance if they choose. The Program Director will also offer support to staff.

The Program Director will inventory the individual's personal funds, belongings and valuables with a second staff member, will return the funds and property to the personal representative or family in a timely manner against a signed receipt, and will document the transfer (see IR-05). Funds will not be kept or used by the agency or staff.

The Program Director will stop billing for the individual from the date of death as required by Medicaid billing rules and will notify the billing staff and the regional office (see GOV-06). The Program Director will also notify the pharmacy and cancel medications and appointments.

The Program Director will tell the Governing Body about the death at its next meeting or sooner. The standing committee will review the death, as it reviews all incidents, for patterns, and will recommend corrective actions. Members involved in the event will not take part in the decision (see GOV-05).

The Governing Body and Program Director will complete a mortality review as part of the quality assurance plan, and will put the findings into action, including changes to the supports of other individuals (see GOV-04).

The Program Director will release health information about the deceased individual only to the personal representative or others the law allows, and only after verifying identity and authority (see IR-04). Requests from the media will be directed to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
The Program Director will close the record, make a final entry and store the record securely for at least 6 years after the date of death (see RC-01 and RC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Call 911, give emergency care, notify the Program Director, preserve information and support other individuals.
Notifies family, proponent, regional office and the DDA coordinator, files the report by the deadline, handles funds and property, and keeps the record.
Confirms the DDA reporting level and deadline, supports the family, and informs the Governing Body.
Assists with review of health records and clinical circumstances.

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support and Behavior Plans
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME] who support individuals in the Community Living – Group Home program; the Program Director; the standing committee
policies.purpose: To make sure that every individual whose behavior requires intervention is supported first through positive, person-centered strategies, and receives the safeguards Maryland requires of licensed community residential providers. This policy also ensures that any behavior plan using restrictive techniques is reviewed and approved before it is used.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals through positive behavior support that addresses the reasons behind challenging behavior, teaches skills, and respects each person's rights, dignity and choices. An individual whose behavior requires intervention will receive the safeguards required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(10). Any behavior plan that uses restrictive techniques must be approved by the agency's standing committee and must comply with the requirements of COMAR 10.22.04 and COMAR 10.22.10 referenced in COMAR 10.22.02.14E(1)(d) before it is implemented. Staff must complete training in the principles of behavior change and management of disruptive behaviors before they perform independent duties (COMAR 10.22.02.11C). Behavior supports are never used as punishment, for staff convenience, or in retaliation. All staff, consultants and volunteers must know and carry out this policy (COMAR 10.22.02.10C).

definitions.definition: A proactive approach that identifies why a behavior occurs, changes the environment and routines, teaches replacement skills, and reinforces desired behavior, without relying on restrictive techniques.

A written plan that is part of the individual's Individual Plan (IP) and addresses challenging behavior. It meets the content and approval requirements of COMAR 10.22.10 and is developed by a qualified professional.
Any intervention that limits an individual's movement, access or freedom, or that uses restraint or medication to control behavior. Details are in BH-02 and BH-03.
The committee described in GOV-05, with equal numbers of agency staff and non-employees (individuals, proponents or community members). It approves behavior plans that use restrictive techniques.
A person who advocates for the individual, such as a family member, guardian or other representative, as described in IR-06.

procedures: Before and during admission (PC-01), the Program Director asks the referring team for any history of challenging behavior, existing behavior plans, crisis plans, and what has and has not worked for the individual. The Program Director records the answers in the individual's record.

During person-centered planning (PC-02), the team identifies communication preferences, triggers, health and sensory factors, and the person's own goals related to behavior. The Program Director records these in the IP.

Where challenging behavior is present or anticipated, the Program Director arranges for a functional assessment by a [QUALIFIED BEHAVIOR PROFESSIONAL] who meets the qualifications required by COMAR 10.22.10. The Program Director documents the referral date and the assessment result.

The team first tries positive and least restrictive strategies, such as environmental changes, schedule changes, skill teaching, choice-making and reinforcement. The team records in the plan which strategies were tried and the results.

Medical, dental, pain, medication side-effect and mental health causes of behavior change are reviewed with the individual's health care providers and the delegating nurse (HW-02, HW-04) before the plan relies on any behavioral intervention.

A written behavior plan is developed with the individual and the proponent. It describes the target behavior in observable terms, the likely function, prevention strategies, replacement skills, staff responses, data collection and review dates. It is written in language staff can follow.

If a plan includes any restrictive technique, the Program Director submits the plan to the standing committee before the technique is used, as described in GOV-05. The plan must also meet the requirements of COMAR 10.22.04 and 10.22.10 that apply to the technique. The plan is not implemented until the committee's approval is recorded.
Committee members do not vote on a behavior plan in which they were involved (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). The Program Director records any recusals in the minutes.
Informed consent from the individual or proponent for the behavior plan is obtained and documented as described in IR-06. Any rights restriction the plan involves follows IR-02.

Before staff work independently with an individual who has a behavior plan, the Program Director trains them on that plan, including the plan's prevention strategies, data forms and the limits on any restrictive techniques. Training is documented with the date, trainer and staff signature.

All new staff complete training in principles of behavior change and management of disruptive behaviors before they perform independent duties (ST-03). The Program Director does not schedule any employee alone with individuals until the training record is complete.
Staff implement the plan as written and record behavior data on the daily documentation forms at the time of the event or by the end of the shift (PC-03).

The [QUALIFIED BEHAVIOR PROFESSIONAL] and the Program Director review behavior data at least monthly. They record whether the plan is working and decide whether to revise, fade or discontinue any restrictive element.
Any use of a restrictive technique is recorded and tracked as described in BH-02 and BH-03, and the Program Director includes the information in the quality assurance data review (GOV-04).

Plan revisions that add or change a restrictive technique return to the standing committee for approval before they are implemented. The Program Director informs the individual and proponent of every revision.
The Program Director reviews each behavior plan with the IP team at least annually and whenever the individual's needs change, and records the review date in the record.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures assessments, plans, committee approvals, consents and staff training are completed before any plan is used; reviews behavior data monthly; reports trends to the committee.
Completes the functional assessment, writes the behavior plan, trains staff on it, and reviews data and revises the plan.
Implement positive supports as written, record behavior data accurately, and report plan problems or any use of a restrictive technique immediately.
Reviews and approves behavior plans that use restrictive techniques before they are implemented and reviews trends.
Reviews health and medication factors that may be contributing to behavior and advises the team.

documentation: Functional assessment and behavior plan in the individual's record
Standing committee minutes and approval record for any plan using restrictive techniques
Informed consent and proponent participation records
Staff training records for principles of behavior change, management of disruptive behaviors and individual plan training
Daily behavior data sheets and monthly data review notes
Plan revision and annual review records

policies.title: Restrictive Interventions, Restraint and Seclusion
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]; the Program Director; the standing committee
policies.purpose: To ensure that restrictive interventions are used only as permitted by Maryland's behavior regulations, are approved in advance when they are part of a plan, are never used as punishment or for convenience, and are tracked and reviewed for every use.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses the least restrictive response that keeps people safe and uses restrictive techniques only as permitted by COMAR 10.22.10. That chapter separately governs the use of restrictive techniques, physical restraint, mechanical restraint and support, and chemical restraint. A behavior plan that uses a restrictive technique must be approved by the standing committee before use (COMAR 10.22.02.14E(1)(d)). Each use of a restrictive technique is recorded and tracked: the individual, the technique, the date and time, whether it was an emergency or planned in the behavior plan, and whether it was effective (COMAR 10.22.02.14B(4)). Restrictive techniques are never used as punishment, for staff convenience, as a substitute for adequate staffing or supports, or in retaliation. [AGENCY NAME] does not use seclusion. Staff must not lock an individual in a room or otherwise prevent a person from leaving a space. Any restraint technique a staff member is not currently trained and authorized to use is not used. In an emergency, staff call 911 rather than improvise a technique.

definitions.definition: A hands-on technique that restricts an individual's movement, as regulated by COMAR 10.22.10.
A device used to restrict an individual's movement, as regulated by COMAR 10.22.10. Devices used for support, as that chapter defines them, are covered by the same chapter.
Medication used to control behavior rather than to treat a diagnosed condition, as regulated by COMAR 10.22.10 and addressed in BH-03.
Placing an individual alone in a room or area from which the person is prevented from leaving. [AGENCY NAME] does not use seclusion.
A use of a restrictive technique that is not planned in an approved behavior plan and is used to prevent imminent serious harm.
A use of a restrictive technique that is written into a committee-approved behavior plan.

procedures: Before any restrictive technique is written into a plan, the Program Director confirms that positive and less restrictive approaches were tried and documents the results (BH-01).

The Program Director and the [QUALIFIED BEHAVIOR PROFESSIONAL] confirm that the specific technique is permitted by the applicable sections of COMAR 10.22.10 and document the section and any required limits, conditions and documentation in the behavior plan.

The Program Director submits the plan to the standing committee. The plan is not implemented until the committee's approval is recorded in the minutes and the individual or proponent's consent is documented (GOV-05, IR-06).

Only staff who have completed training on the specific technique and the individual's plan may use it. The Program Director keeps a list of authorized staff, with training dates, in the personnel and training records (ST-04, ST-06).
Staff use a technique only for the reason and in the manner stated in the plan. They stop as soon as the immediate risk has ended.

In an emergency, staff first call for help, remove other individuals and hazards, and use only techniques for which they are trained and which are allowed under COMAR 10.22.10. If a person is in medical distress or the risk cannot be controlled, staff call 911 immediately (HW-04).

No staff member may secure an individual in a locked room, prevent a person from leaving a room, or use any other form of seclusion. If a staff member is directed to do so, the staff member must refuse and report it to the Program Director or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at once.
After any use, staff check the individual for injury and distress, obtain medical care when needed, and write a factual record before the end of the shift.

The record of each use states: the individual; the technique; the date and start and end times; whether it was emergency or planned; what happened before, during and after; staff involved; any injuries; and whether the technique was effective. The Program Director enters the information in the restrictive technique tracking log required by the quality assurance system.

Staff notify the Program Director immediately after any emergency use or any use outside the approved plan. The Program Director notifies the proponent as soon as possible and no later than the next business day, and documents the notice.

The Program Director treats every emergency use, injury or suspected misuse as a reportable incident and handles it under BH-05. If misuse may be abuse, BH-04 applies and the employee may be removed from direct duties pending investigation.
The Program Director holds a debriefing with staff and, as appropriate, the individual after each use to identify triggers and ways to prevent a recurrence, and records the outcome.
After an emergency use, the Program Director requests an expedited review of the behavior plan by the [QUALIFIED BEHAVIOR PROFESSIONAL] and brings repeated emergency use to the standing committee.

The Program Director reviews the tracking log monthly and presents totals and trends by individual, technique, staff and time of day to the standing committee and in the quality assurance data review (GOV-04, GOV-05).

The committee reviews effectiveness and decides whether to continue, change or discontinue each approved technique, and the Program Director records the decision and communicates it to staff and the proponent.
The Program Director audits technique use against plans quarterly to confirm that no technique was used without approval and that all training and consent records are current.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures no technique is used without an approved plan and trained staff; maintains the tracking log; notifies proponents; submits trends to the committee.
Ensures resources and staffing are adequate to avoid reliance on restrictive techniques and takes action on any misuse.
Use only approved, trained techniques, document each use before the end of the shift, and report misuse.
Approves plans using restrictive techniques and reviews tracking data and effectiveness.
Confirms the technique is permitted, trains staff, and reviews and revises plans after use.

documentation: Restrictive technique tracking log (individual, technique, date and time, emergency or planned, effectiveness)
Incident reports for each emergency use or injury
Standing committee approvals and trend reviews
Staff training and authorization records for each technique
Proponent notification and consent records
Debriefing notes and monthly and quarterly audit results

policies.title: Medications Used to Modify Behavior and Restrictive Technique Monitoring
policies.applies_to: The Program Director, delegating nurse, medication technicians and all staff who administer or monitor medication or document restrictive techniques; the standing committee
policies.purpose: To ensure that any medication used to modify challenging behavior is prescribed, consented to, administered, monitored and reviewed as required by COMAR 10.22.10, and that medications and restrictive techniques are monitored through the quality assurance system.
policies.policy: Medications used to modify challenging behavior are used only as permitted by COMAR 10.22.10, which governs the use of medications to modify challenging behavior and the monitoring of the use of those medications and of restrictive techniques. Medication is never used as punishment, for staff convenience, or in place of adequate supports. The quality assurance system must record each medication or technique used, the date and time, whether it was an emergency or planned, and whether it meets the behavior plan's goals (COMAR 10.22.02.14B(4)). The standing committee reviews the resulting trends.

definitions.definition: A medication prescribed or given to control or change challenging behavior, as regulated by COMAR 10.22.10, as distinct from medication prescribed to treat a diagnosed medical or psychiatric condition.
Use of a medication or technique that is not planned in the individual's approved behavior plan.
Use of a medication or technique that is included in a behavior plan approved as required by BH-01.
The registered nurse who delegates medication administration to medication technicians and oversees health care coordination (HW-02).

procedures: When a prescriber proposes a medication to modify behavior, the Program Director or delegating nurse asks the prescriber for the diagnosis, target behavior, expected benefit, side effects, and review date, and records them in the individual's record.

Before the medication is started, the Program Director confirms that the behavior plan addresses the medication and the requirements of COMAR 10.22.10 that apply to it, and that positive and less restrictive supports have been tried (BH-01).
The Program Director obtains and documents informed consent from the individual or proponent, with an explanation of risks and alternatives in understandable language (IR-06).

Where the plan or applicable rules require standing committee review or approval of the medication, the Program Director presents the plan to the committee and does not start the medication until approval is recorded (GOV-05).
Only certified medication technicians working under the delegating nurse's oversight administer the medication, exactly as prescribed (HW-01).

PRN or emergency doses for behavior are given only under a written prescriber order and a written protocol that identifies the behaviors, the alternatives to try first, and when to call the prescriber or 911. Staff do not use a PRN dose for staff convenience.

Each time a behavior medication is given, staff record on the medication administration record (MAR) and in the daily notes the date and time, the behavior that led to the dose if given PRN, whether it was planned or an emergency, and the individual's response.

The Program Director enters each use of a medication or restrictive technique in the monitoring log, with the medication or technique, date and time, planned or emergency, and whether it met the behavior plan's goals (COMAR 10.22.02.14B(4)).

The delegating nurse monitors the individual for side effects, changes in alertness, movement, appetite, sleep and mood, and arranges necessary laboratory tests and prescriber follow-up. Findings are recorded in the health record (HW-02, HW-03).

Staff report suspected side effects, a medication error, refusal, or an unplanned emergency use to the Program Director and nurse immediately. The Program Director handles medication errors and unplanned emergency uses as reportable incidents under BH-05.
The [QUALIFIED BEHAVIOR PROFESSIONAL] reviews behavior data together with medication data at least monthly and records whether the medication and the plan are meeting their goals.

The Program Director asks the prescriber to review the need for the medication, including dose reduction where appropriate, at the interval the prescriber and team set, and records the review date and outcome.

The Program Director compiles monthly totals of all uses of behavior medications and restrictive techniques by individual, type, planned vs. emergency, time of day and staff, and brings them to the standing committee (GOV-04, GOV-05).

The committee reviews the trends, identifies patterns or deficient practices, and recommends corrective action. The Program Director records the actions and completes them by the date the committee sets.
The Program Director updates the proponent and the IP team when a behavior medication is started, changed or discontinued and records the date and the method of notification.
The delegating nurse and Program Director audit MARs against the behavior plan and tracking log quarterly, and correct any gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures consents, approvals, tracking entries and follow-up are completed; reports data to the committee.
Monitors medication effects, communicates with prescribers, and oversees technician administration.
Administer behavior medications only as ordered and document each dose and each PRN use.
Evaluates whether medication and plan are meeting the goals and recommends changes.
Reviews trend data and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Prescriber orders and PRN protocols
Informed consent and any committee approval
MAR and daily notes for behavior medications
Monitoring log of medications and techniques (date and time, emergency or planned, goal met)
Nurse monitoring notes and prescriber review records
Monthly trend reports and committee minutes

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]; the Program Director; [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]; the standing committee
policies.purpose: To protect every individual from abuse, neglect and exploitation; to ensure that every suspected case is immediately reported to the proper authorities and investigated; and to protect people who report.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect and exploitation. Every incident must be reported and investigated under the DDA's incident reporting procedures (COMAR 10.22.02.10A(7)); the current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII) governs the incident categories, report recipients, deadlines and forms. Reports are made to the local department of social services (Adult Protective Services) and to the DDA and OHCQ as PORII requires. Agency staff are treated as required reporters under this policy and must also comply with any mandatory reporting law that applies to them individually. No one may retaliate against a person who reports in good faith (COMAR 10.22.02.10A(5)). [AGENCY NAME] does not employ or contract with anyone whose criminal history indicates behavior potentially harmful to individuals (COMAR 10.22.02.11B). All staff, consultants and volunteers must know and carry out this policy (COMAR 10.22.02.10C).

definitions.definition: Any act that causes or may cause physical, sexual or emotional harm to an individual, including hitting, rough handling, sexual contact, threats, humiliation, and misuse of restraint, as the current PORII defines it.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, medical care, food or other supports an individual needs for health and safety.
Taking or misusing an individual's money, property, benefits or labor for the benefit of someone else.
The DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, as currently in effect.
Adult Protective Services at the local department of social services.

procedures: Any staff member who sees, hears about or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation first makes sure the individual is safe, separates the individual from any alleged abuser, and calls 911 if there is an emergency, injury or crime.

The staff member obtains medical care for any injury or health concern and tells the responding providers about the suspected cause (HW-04). Staff do not clean or disturb evidence if a crime may have occurred.

The staff member immediately notifies the Program Director, or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] if the Program Director is the person involved or unavailable. A staff member never needs permission from a supervisor to report to outside authorities and may report directly.

Within the time the PORII sets for the incident category, the Program Director or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reports to the DDA and OHCQ using the current PORII forms and process, and to the local department of social services (APS) at [LOCAL DSS PHONE]. If the supervisor does not act, the staff member makes the report directly.
Any person may also report to the OHCQ complaint line at 410-402-8100 or 877-402-8220. The number is posted in the home where individuals and staff can see it (IR-03).
The Program Director notifies the proponent and the support coordinator of the incident and the steps taken, as the PORII requires, and records the date, time and method.

If the alleged abuser is an employee, contractor or volunteer, the Program Director immediately removes the person from direct contact with all individuals pending the investigation. Removal is not discipline and is documented.
The Program Director preserves records, schedules, notes and any physical evidence and secures a written statement from each witness before the end of the shift where possible.

The agency investigates under BH-05, or cooperates with the investigating agency as PORII directs. Staff do not interview the individual in a way that could influence the individual's account, and an individual is never pressed to change an account.
The agency takes protective measures for the individual, including changes in staffing, supervision, counseling or medical follow-up, and records them in the record and the IP (PC-02).

No one may retaliate against an individual, staff member or other person who reports or participates in an investigation. Retaliation is grounds for discipline, up to and including termination, and the Program Director reports any alleged retaliation to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] immediately.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews the investigation findings and decides on discipline, retraining, termination or other corrective actions, and refers findings to licensing boards, registries or law enforcement as required by law and PORII (ST-02, ST-07).

Prevention: before hire, the agency completes the criminal history and registry checks described in ST-02 and does not employ or contract with anyone whose history indicates behavior potentially harmful to individuals (COMAR 10.22.02.11B).

Prevention: all staff are trained during orientation and annually on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation, on individuals' rights, and on this policy (ST-03, IR-01). Training is documented with date and signature.

Prevention: the Program Director reviews each individual's risk factors, including communication limits, dependence on others for personal care and finances, and past victimization, and addresses them in supervision and the IP. Individuals are taught, in ways they understand, how to say no and whom to tell.

The standing committee reviews every incident, including all abuse, neglect and exploitation reports, to identify deficient practices and recommend corrective action (GOV-05), and the quality assurance system tracks trends (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Protect individuals, report suspicions immediately, cooperate with investigations, and never retaliate.
Ensures that required reports are made on time, individuals are protected, accused staff are removed from contact, and investigations are completed.
Receives reports involving the Program Director, decides corrective action, and ensures cooperation with authorities.
Reviews all incidents and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Incident reports and PORII forms submitted to DDA and OHCQ
Records of reports to APS and law enforcement
Investigation file: statements, evidence, findings, corrective actions
Notification records to proponents and support coordinators
Staff training records on abuse, neglect, exploitation and rights
Background check and registry records

policies.title: Reportable Incidents and Investigations
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]; the Program Director; [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]; the standing committee
policies.purpose: To ensure that every incident, including life-threatening conditions, is reported to the required authorities, investigated, reviewed by the standing committee, and used to prevent recurrence, and that [AGENCY NAME] responds correctly to OHCQ investigations.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports and investigates all incidents, including life-threatening conditions, under the DDA's procedures on reportable incidents (COMAR 10.22.02.10A(7)). The current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII) is the controlling source for incident levels, report recipients, deadlines and forms, and the Program Director keeps the current version available to all staff. The standing committee reviews the incident protocol and all incidents to identify deficient practices and recommend corrective action (COMAR 10.22.02.14E(1)(b)-(c)). OHCQ, as the DDA's agent, may investigate complaints and incidents through announced or unannounced visits (COMAR 10.22.02.04D); investigations of immediate jeopardy (Priority 1) begin within 2 working days (COMAR 10.22.02.03). A plan of correction is due at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving the findings (COMAR 10.22.02.04E).

definitions.definition: An event or condition that affects an individual's health, safety, rights or well-being and that is reportable under the current PORII, including life-threatening conditions, injuries, abuse, neglect, exploitation, missing persons and unplanned use of restrictive techniques.
The DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, as currently in effect.
A situation OHCQ assigns the highest priority because of serious risk to individuals. OHCQ begins Priority 1 investigations within 2 working days.
The written plan [AGENCY NAME] submits to OHCQ stating how and by when each cited deficiency will be corrected.

procedures: Staff first protect the individual: provide first aid, call 911 where needed, remove hazards, and follow HW-04 for medical changes and emergencies.

Staff immediately notify the Program Director, or the on-call administrator at [PHONE] after hours, of any incident. They do not wait until the end of the shift for incidents involving injury, abuse, neglect, missing persons or a life-threatening condition.

The Program Director determines the PORII category and the required report recipients and deadlines using the current PORII. If the category is unclear, the Program Director treats it as the more serious category and consults [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

The Program Director or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits the report to the DDA and OHCQ on the current PORII forms and process within the PORII deadline. Any additional notice to law enforcement, APS (BH-04) and the proponent is made at the same time or as PORII requires, and the date, time and method are recorded.

The staff member who witnessed or discovered the incident writes a factual incident report before the end of the shift, with the date, time, place, people involved, what happened, actions taken and notifications made. Opinions and conclusions are kept out of the report.
The Program Director assigns an investigator who is not involved in the incident and who is trained to investigate. If the Program Director is involved, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] assigns the investigator.

The investigator secures evidence, interviews the individual with appropriate communication supports, witnesses and staff, reviews records, and writes a report of findings and conclusions by the PORII deadline for investigations.

The agency cooperates fully with any outside investigation by OHCQ, law enforcement or APS, makes records and staff available, and does not interfere with or retaliate for a report or participation (COMAR 10.22.02.10A(5)).

The Program Director implements immediate protective measures and corrective action, such as retraining, supervision changes, environmental repair or plan revisions, and records the person responsible and the completion date for each.
The Program Director reports required follow-up and final investigation information to the DDA and OHCQ by the deadlines in the PORII.

The standing committee reviews all incidents, and at least annually the incident protocol itself, to identify deficient practices and recommend corrective action. Committee members who were involved in an incident do not decide on it (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). The Program Director records the review and actions in the minutes (GOV-05).

The Program Director enters each incident in the incident log and includes counts, types, locations, times and trends in the quality assurance data review (GOV-04). The Program Director responds promptly to any trend indicating risk to health or safety.
If OHCQ notifies [AGENCY NAME] of a complaint or incident investigation, the Program Director immediately informs [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], provides access to the home and records, and follows GOV-09.

After OHCQ gives its findings, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits a plan of correction at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving the findings, or sooner if OHCQ requires. If an extension is needed, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] asks OHCQ promptly; the OHCQ Director may grant an extension of up to 30 days.

If OHCQ finds the POC unacceptable, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits a revised plan of correction within 10 working days (COMAR 10.22.02.04F), and the Program Director carries out and documents each corrective step by the stated date.
The Program Director reviews open incidents and corrective actions weekly until closed and reports their status to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] monthly.

responsibilities.duty: Protect the individual, report any incident immediately, and write a factual incident report before the end of the shift.
Determines the PORII category, makes timely reports, assigns the investigator, implements corrective action and maintains the incident log.
Ensures accurate and timely reporting, handles incidents involving the Program Director, and submits any plan of correction.
Reviews the incident protocol and all incidents, and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Incident reports and PORII submissions with dates and times of notice
Investigation reports and corrective action records
Incident log and trend analyses
Standing committee minutes on incident review
OHCQ correspondence, findings, plans of correction and extension requests
Proponent and support coordinator notification records

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Program Director, and on-call administrators of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect individuals who leave the home or a supervised setting without staff knowledge, by providing for prevention, an immediate search, police notification and required reports.
policies.policy: A missing person is a reportable incident under the DDA incident reporting procedure (COMAR 10.22.02.10A(7)), and the current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII) controls the incident category and the reporting deadline. [AGENCY NAME] ensures that each individual's IP addresses elopement risk (COMAR 10.22.02.10A(1)) and that staff know the plan and carry it out. Individuals have the right to come and go consistent with their IP; an individual who is out of the home by choice and in accordance with the IP is not a missing person. The standing committee reviews every incident, including each missing person incident (COMAR 10.22.02.14E(1)(c)).

definitions.definition: An individual whose whereabouts are unknown and who is not where the IP, schedule or supervision plan requires, or who has left without agreed-upon notice, as the PORII defines.
An individual leaving the home, vehicle or activity without staff knowledge or permission when the IP requires supervision.
The part of the IP that identifies the person's risk, triggers, supports and the steps staff must take.
A person who advocates for the individual, such as a family member, guardian or other representative.

procedures: During admission and person-centered planning, the Program Director and team assess each person's elopement risk, including past episodes, habits, favorite places, wandering patterns, traffic and water awareness, and ability to give identifying information. The assessment and plan are recorded in the IP (PC-01, PC-02).

The Program Director keeps a current identification sheet for each individual at risk, including a recent photograph, physical description, clothing description, health needs, medications, communication ability, likely places and the proponent's phone number. Staff can reach it at once in the home.

The elopement risk plan sets the level of supervision, door and environmental safeguards that are consistent with the person's rights (IR-01, IR-02, HE-01), and staffing needed. The Program Director trains staff on the plan before they work alone with the individual.

When staff discover an individual is missing, they immediately search the home, grounds, vehicle and nearby places named in the IP, while keeping all other individuals supervised. The staff member calls for additional staff or the on-call administrator at [PHONE] to assist.

Staff call 911 immediately if the IP identifies the person as high risk, if the person has medical or safety needs, or if the person is not found after the initial search of the home and grounds. The staff member gives the person's name, description, clothing, medical needs, and last-seen time and place.
Staff immediately notify the Program Director or the on-call administrator, who joins the search and directs the response. The Program Director ensures enough staff remain with the other individuals.
The Program Director notifies the proponent as soon as possible and records the time and method. The notice continues until the person is found.

The Program Director reports the incident to the DDA and OHCQ, including the DDA regional office, using the current PORII category, forms and deadline, and records the date and time of the report (BH-05, RC-03).
Staff keep a written log of the search: times, places checked, people contacted, police contact and case number, and who did what.

When the person is found, staff make sure the person is safe, ask in a respectful way what happened, and arrange for medical examination if there is any sign of injury, exposure, or other health concern (HW-04). Staff inform the police, proponent, DDA and OHCQ that the person has been found.

If there is any indication of abuse, neglect or exploitation while the person was missing, or if inadequate supervision contributed, the Program Director follows BH-04 and removes involved staff from direct duties pending investigation.
The Program Director completes the incident report and investigation under BH-05, including what led to the person leaving, whether the plan was followed, and corrective action.
The IP team meets promptly after any episode to review and revise the elopement risk plan, the individual's supports, the environment and staffing, and records the revisions (PC-02, ST-01).
The standing committee reviews each missing person incident and the corrective actions (GOV-05), and the quality assurance system tracks the number of episodes and trends (GOV-04).
The Program Director conducts an annual drill for staff on the missing person response and records the date and results. Staff who miss it are trained before their next independent shift.

responsibilities.duty: Know each person's elopement plan, supervise as planned, search at once, call 911 when required and notify the Program Director.
Maintains identification sheets and risk plans, directs the search, makes notifications and PORII reports, and ensures post-incident review.
Responds after hours, assists the search and ensures staffing for others in the home.
Reviews every missing person incident and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment and plan in the IP
Identification sheet with current photograph
Search log and 911 or police case number
Incident report and PORII submission
Notification records (proponent, DDA regional office, OHCQ)
Post-incident IP team review and committee minutes
Staff training and drill records

policies.title: Residential Environment and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: All licensed Community Living – Group Home sites operated by [AGENCY NAME], including the Program Director, Home Managers, direct support staff, maintenance personnel and contractors
policies.purpose: To make sure every home operated by [AGENCY NAME] is safe, in good repair, accessible to the people who live there, and a real home in the community rather than an institutional or isolating setting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will operate each home in compliance with local zoning (except as provided in Health-General §7-603), local and State building codes, and life-safety requirements. Each home will be free of hazards and kept in good repair. Each home will serve no more than four residents unless DDA has previously approved a different number. Each resident will have a private bedroom; a resident shares a bedroom only by his or her own choice. Bedroom doors will lock, and the resident will control who enters. Hot water will not exceed 110°F unless every resident of the home can regulate it safely and this is documented in each resident's Individual Plan (IP). The home will be accessible to the needs of the residents who live there and will not be gated or isolated from the surrounding community. Any change to a resident's control over his or her space or privacy must rest on a specific assessed need and be documented in that person's IP.

definitions.definition: The residence listed on the DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites (MDH Form DD.ADD.1.0) where [AGENCY NAME] provides Community Living – Group Home services.
Any condition that could reasonably cause injury or illness, such as a trip hazard, a fire hazard, an unsafe water temperature, a broken railing or a damaged electrical cord.
A residence that the provider owns, leases or controls, where the federal HCBS settings requirements for privacy, lockable doors and control of personal space apply.

A feature that separates residents from the broader community or makes the home resemble a facility, such as a gate, a facility-style sign, or a location next to other sites operated by the provider that creates heightened scrutiny.

procedures: Before a site is proposed to DDA, the Program Director confirms that the property complies with local zoning (including any applicable Health-General §7-603 provision), and obtains local building, occupancy and fire inspections where applicable. Copies are kept in the site file.

The Program Director completes the site section of DDA Addendum DD.ADD.1.0, including the capacity requested, the proposed occupancy date, the Community Settings Rule attestation, and the answer to whether the site is wheelchair accessible. The Program Director does not sign the attestation until the DDA New Site Visit Checklist (Community Settings Rule) has been completed internally and any deficiency has been corrected.

The Program Director uses the DDA New Site Visit Checklist (Community Settings Rule) to review the site for institutional or isolating characteristics and for heightened scrutiny factors, including proximity to [AGENCY NAME]'s other sites. Findings and corrections are recorded in the site file.
The home's capacity is set at no more than four residents unless DDA has previously approved another number in writing. The Program Director keeps that approval in the site file.
Each resident is given a private bedroom. A resident shares a bedroom only when the resident chooses to, and that choice is recorded in the IP and the residency file.

Each bedroom door is fitted with a lock. The resident holds a key or other means of entry, and staff access is limited to what is documented. Any limit on a resident's lock or key, or on access to his or her space, is allowed only when the IP records a specific assessed need, the less intrusive methods tried, and the time-limited plan for review. Such limits follow IR-02.
Residents decorate and furnish their bedrooms with their own belongings as they choose. Staff do not remove or restrict personal items except under IR-02.

The Home Manager completes a documented home safety walk-through at least monthly, and after any incident of damage or injury, using the site safety checklist. The walk-through covers floors, stairs, railings, electrical cords and outlets, appliances, heating, ventilation, windows, locks, exits, outdoor areas, and the condition of furniture and equipment.

The Home Manager records every hazard or repair need on the work order log on the day it is found. Hazards that present an immediate risk are made safe the same day, and the resident is moved away from the risk until repaired. The Program Director reviews open work orders weekly until closed.

Each month the Home Manager checks hot water at representative taps used by residents with a calibrated thermometer, and records the readings. The water heater is set so that water at the tap does not exceed 110°F. A higher temperature is allowed only if the IP of every resident in the home documents that the resident can regulate the water safely. A tap above 110°F without that documentation is reported to the Program Director on the day found and corrected immediately.

At admission, and whenever a resident's condition or mobility changes, the Program Director and the resident's team review the home's accessibility for that person (entrances, doorways, bathrooms, bedrooms, kitchen, and routes outdoors). Needed modifications, such as ramps, grab bars, roll-in showers or door widening, are written into the IP and funded and scheduled through the proper approval channels. If the home cannot meet an accessibility need, the issue is raised under PC-01 or PC-05 and does not result in a resident being confined or denied access to parts of the home.

[AGENCY NAME] does not install perimeter fencing, gates, or exterior locks that prevent residents from leaving the home. Doors that residents are permitted to use are operable from inside without a key. Any exit-related safeguard for an individual resident is handled only through IR-02, BH-02 and BH-06.

The home is located and kept so that residents have access to the surrounding community, including public transportation, shops, places of worship and recreation. No exterior signage or vehicle markings identify the home as a facility for people with disabilities.

Residents have access to common areas, the kitchen, the laundry and outdoor space at any time, consistent with their IP. Visitors are welcome at times of the resident's choosing, consistent with IR-01.

Before any renovation, change in layout or change in the number of residents, the Program Director confirms that local building and life-safety requirements are still met and notifies DDA and OHCQ as required under GOV-08.
The Program Director reports the results of home environment reviews, open hazards and accessibility modifications to the Governing Body each quarter under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures compliance with zoning, building, life-safety and DDA site requirements; completes DD.ADD.1.0 and the Community Settings Rule review; approves accessibility modifications; reviews work orders weekly.
Performs monthly walk-throughs and water temperature checks; logs and escalates hazards and repairs; protects residents' privacy, lockable doors and use of the whole home.
Report hazards immediately; respect residents' bedrooms and belongings; never block exits or lock residents out of areas of the home.
Provides the resources for repairs and accessibility modifications and reviews quarterly environment reports.
Complete repairs promptly according to the work order log and comply with this policy.

documentation: Zoning, building, occupancy and fire inspection records in the site file
Completed DDA Addendum DD.ADD.1.0 and DDA New Site Visit Checklist (Community Settings Rule)
DDA approval for any capacity above four, if applicable
Monthly home safety walk-through checklists
Work order log and repair records
Monthly hot water temperature log and any IP documentation allowing a higher temperature
Accessibility reviews and modification records
IP entries on shared bedrooms by choice and any modification to privacy or access

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Fire Drills
policies.applies_to: All licensed sites, all staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants, and every resident of [AGENCY NAME]'s homes
policies.purpose: To protect residents during fires, severe weather, utility failures, and other emergencies and disasters by maintaining a written fire evacuation plan and an all-hazards emergency plan that is practiced, reviewed and shared.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will maintain, at each home, a written fire evacuation plan, adequate smoke detectors, and working, updated fire extinguishers. [AGENCY NAME] will also maintain a written disaster and emergency evacuation plan, and conduct sufficient evacuation drills, for all emergencies and disasters. The emergency plan covers procedures before, during and after an emergency, evacuation or 72-hour shelter-in-place, an annual practice drill coordinated with local emergency planners, an after-action report and improvement plan, identification for each resident with health and contact information, notification of families and the DDA regional office, staff coverage and recall, continuity of operations, off-site backup of records, and sharing of the plan with local emergency management. [AGENCY NAME] will give an executive summary of the plan to families on request. All staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants must know and carry out this policy.

definitions.definition: A written plan, specific to each home, showing exits, routes, assembly points, and the assistance each resident needs to leave the home safely.
Remaining in the home during an emergency, with the supplies and supports to sustain residents for at least 72 hours.
A written review after a drill or actual emergency stating what worked, what did not, and the corrective actions, owners and due dates.
Arrangements to keep services, medications, staffing, records and billing functioning during and after an emergency.

procedures: The Program Director, with the Home Manager, writes a fire evacuation plan for each home. It shows two exit routes from every area where residents sleep or spend time, an outside assembly point, and a floor plan posted in a visible location. The plan is reviewed when a resident's mobility changes, when a resident moves in or out, or when the layout changes.

Each resident's IP and emergency evacuation information state the help the person needs to evacuate (for example, wheelchair assistance, cueing, or a hearing or vision aid). The Home Manager updates this information within 24 hours of any change in the resident's needs.

The Home Manager installs smoke detectors in all sleeping areas and on each level of the home and keeps them working. Detectors are tested at least monthly, and batteries or units are replaced as needed. Tests are logged with date, initials and results.

The Home Manager places fire extinguishers in accessible locations, checks them monthly for charge and condition, and has them serviced and tagged by a qualified vendor as the manufacturer and local fire code require. Any extinguisher that is missing, discharged or past due is replaced the same day.

The Program Director contacts the local fire marshal to confirm the required frequency and form of fire drills for each home. COMAR sets no drill frequency in the text relied on here. [AGENCY NAME] adopts the fire marshal's requirement, and in no case fewer drills than are sufficient to allow every resident and staff member to practice. The fire marshal's answer is kept in the site file.

The Home Manager schedules fire evacuation drills so that they cover all shifts, including overnight, with different staff, and under varied conditions (for example, one exit blocked). Residents take part according to their IP. No drill is run in a way that frightens a resident or puts him or her at risk.

After each drill the Home Manager records the date, time, shift, staff present, residents who participated, time to evacuate, problems found and corrective action. The Program Director reviews each drill record within 7 days and ensures corrective action is done.

The Program Director writes an emergency plan for each home covering fire, severe weather, flooding, power or water outage, loss of heat or cooling, gas leak, infectious disease outbreak, loss of staff, and the need to evacuate or shelter in place. The plan states what is done before, during and after each emergency.

The plan provides for evacuation to a named alternate site and for sheltering in place for at least 72 hours, including water, food (with modified diets per HE-04), a 72-hour supply of medications and treatments, medical equipment and power needs, hygiene supplies, flashlights, batteries, and cash. The Home Manager checks and rotates emergency supplies every quarter.

Each resident has an emergency identification card or wristband or equivalent that lists name, diagnoses, allergies, medications, physician, emergency contacts and guardian or proponent information. A copy goes with the resident in any evacuation, along with the medication administration records and the resident's emergency medical information, which is kept so that emergency personnel can reach it readily.

The plan states the role of each resident, family member and legal representative, and identifies how medical needs will be met if a resident goes to a public shelter, such as who accompanies the resident and what equipment and medicines go along.

The plan includes a call tree and instructions to notify families and legal representatives, the DDA regional office, OHCQ if required, and the Program Director. The Home Manager makes these notifications as soon as residents are safe, and no later than the same day. Events that also meet the definition of a reportable incident are handled under BH-05.

The plan includes a staff recall list and the process for ensuring staff coverage during an emergency, so that 24-hour services continue as required under ST-01. Staff contact lists are updated at least quarterly.

The plan includes continuity of operations: how medications, MARs, individual records, payroll and billing records will be preserved or reached, with off-site backup of electronic records under RC-02. The Program Director verifies each quarter that off-site backup is working.

Each year the Program Director conducts a practice drill of the emergency plan (beyond fire drills), coordinated with local emergency planners, and completes a written after-action report and improvement plan within 30 days. Corrective actions are assigned to named staff with due dates, and the Program Director confirms completion.

The Program Director shares the emergency plan with the local emergency management agency each year and when it is revised, and keeps proof of delivery. An executive summary is prepared and provided to a family or legal representative on request, within 10 business days.

All new staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants are trained on the fire evacuation plan and the emergency plan before working independently, and all staff are retrained at least annually and after any plan revision. Training is recorded in the personnel file under ST-06.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and approves plans; coordinates with the fire marshal and local emergency management; conducts the annual practice drill; approves after-action reports and tracks corrective actions.
Maintains detectors, extinguishers and supplies; schedules and records drills; keeps resident evacuation information and emergency ID current; trains staff.
Know the plans, take part in drills, assist residents safely, and take emergency information and medications when evacuating.
Funds emergency resources and reviews drill and after-action results at least annually.

documentation: Written fire evacuation plan and posted floor plan for each home
Smoke detector test log and extinguisher inspection and service records
Fire marshal correspondence on drill requirements
Fire drill records, with corrective actions
Written emergency plan, alternate site agreements and emergency supply checklists
Resident emergency ID information and evacuation assistance needs
Staff recall list and notification call tree
Annual practice drill after-action report and improvement plan
Proof of delivery of the plan to local emergency management and records of executive summaries given to families
Emergency training records for staff

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants working in [AGENCY NAME]'s homes, and residents' households
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents and staff by applying standard precautions and the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard in every home.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will implement State and federally required safety precautions, infection control and standard precautions in every home. [AGENCY NAME] will maintain a written OSHA exposure control plan, offer hepatitis B vaccination to staff with occupational exposure, and provide bloodborne pathogen training before independent duties and annually afterward. Communicable disease training is provided within 3 months of hire. All staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants must know and carry out this policy.

definitions.definition: Basic infection prevention practices applied with every person at all times, including hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, safe handling of sharps, and cleaning and disinfection.
The written plan required by 29 CFR 1910.1030(c) that identifies who may be exposed to blood or other potentially infectious materials and how exposure is minimized.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials during the performance of duties.
Gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and similar items that act as a barrier between the worker and infectious material.

procedures: The Program Director writes and approves an exposure control plan consistent with 29 CFR 1910.1030(c). The plan lists job categories with possible exposure, the tasks involved, the methods of control, and the post-exposure evaluation process. The Program Director reviews and updates it at least annually and when tasks or procedures change.

Before independent duties, every new employee completes bloodborne pathogens training that meets OSHA requirements. The training covers modes of transmission, the exposure control plan, PPE, vaccination, and what to do after an exposure. Staff then repeat the training at least annually. Completion is recorded under ST-03, ST-04 and ST-06.
Within 3 months of hire, all staff complete DDA-approved communicable disease training. Training dates are logged in the personnel file.

[AGENCY NAME] offers the hepatitis B vaccination series, at no cost to the employee, to every employee with occupational exposure, within 10 working days of initial assignment as provided in 29 CFR 1910.1030(f). An employee who declines signs a declination form, and may accept later. Records are kept confidential in a medical file separate from the personnel file.

All staff follow standard precautions with every resident. Staff perform hand hygiene before and after contact with a resident, before preparing food, before giving medication, after using the toilet, after removing gloves, and after contact with bodily fluids. Soap, water, paper towels and alcohol-based hand rub are always stocked.

The Home Manager stocks each home with gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, spill kits, sharps containers, biohazard bags, and disinfectant approved for the pathogens of concern. Supplies are checked weekly and replenished the same day when low.

Staff wear gloves and other PPE whenever contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items is expected. Staff remove PPE properly, discard it in the correct container, and perform hand hygiene afterwards.

Blood and body fluid spills are cleaned immediately by trained staff wearing PPE, using a disinfectant effective against bloodborne pathogens. Contaminated waste is placed in labeled biohazard bags and disposed of according to local rules. Contaminated laundry is handled with gloves and as little as possible, and washed separately in hot water with detergent.

Sharps, such as lancets and needles, are never recapped or bent. They are placed in labeled, puncture-resistant sharps containers, and the containers are replaced when three-quarters full and disposed of according to local rules.

Staff clean and disinfect high-touch surfaces (door handles, light switches, remote controls, handrails, bathrooms, kitchen surfaces) daily and as needed, and clean shared equipment (thermometers, blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, wheelchairs) between uses. The Home Manager keeps a cleaning schedule and checks that it is followed.
Staff follow safe food handling and kitchen sanitation practices described in HE-04, and do not prepare food while ill with vomiting or diarrhea.

Staff who have symptoms of a communicable illness report to the Home Manager before the shift and follow work restrictions under ST-05. The Home Manager arranges replacement coverage so that residents are not left without required staffing.

When a resident develops signs of infection (for example fever, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or wound drainage), staff notify the Home Manager and the resident's health care provider, record the observations, follow the provider's orders, and implement isolation or cohorting measures reasonable for the home while respecting the resident's rights. Change-of-condition actions follow HW-03 and HW-04.

Staff encourage and help residents with hand hygiene, personal hygiene, oral care, immunizations according to their health care provider's advice, and annual health screenings, with the resident's consent under IR-06.

After any exposure incident, the employee washes the area immediately, reports to the Home Manager at once, and receives a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost, consistent with 29 CFR 1910.1030(f). The Program Director records the circumstances, completes an incident report under BH-05 where required, and reviews whether the exposure control plan needs changes.

For outbreaks or reportable communicable diseases, the Program Director notifies the local health department as required by law, and the Home Manager notifies families and legal representatives and the DDA regional office when required under RC-03. Hazard communication and labeling follow 29 CFR 1910.1030(g).
The Program Director reviews infection events, exposure incidents, cleaning audits and training compliance each quarter, and reports trends to the Governing Body under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and reviews the exposure control plan; ensures training, vaccination offers and supplies; handles exposure incidents and outbreak reporting.
Keeps supplies and cleaning schedules; supervises standard precautions; sends ill staff home; coordinates replacement coverage.
Follow standard precautions every time; use PPE; report symptoms, exposures and spills immediately.
Advises on infection control, health teaching and resident-specific precautions.

documentation: Written OSHA exposure control plan with annual review record
Bloodborne pathogens and communicable disease training records
Hepatitis B vaccination offers, acceptances and declination forms (confidential medical file)
Cleaning schedules and supply checklists
Exposure incident reports and post-exposure follow-up records
Outbreak notifications to health authorities and families
Quarterly infection control review summaries

policies.title: Food, Nutrition and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All residents, Home Managers, direct support staff and the Delegating Nurse of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To support residents in choosing what, when and where they eat, while keeping them safe through accurate allergy records and diet orders that are carried out as written.
policies.policy: Residents will have access to food at any time. Any restriction on access to food will be allowed only when it is based on a specific assessed need and documented as a modification in the resident's Individual Plan (IP) under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi). Each resident's allergies and diagnoses will be recorded in the individual record. Diet orders and modified textures will be written in the IP, follow the physician's order, and be carried out by all staff. This manual relies on the cited COMAR sections, which do not contain a specific rule on diets; this policy is therefore built on the IP, physician orders and the resident's rights.

definitions.definition: A diet ordered by a physician or other licensed practitioner that changes the content, texture, consistency, or amount of food or liquid, such as a pureed, mechanical soft, thickened liquid, diabetic, low-sodium, or allergen-free diet.

definitions.term: Access to food at any time
definitions.definition: The resident can get meals and snacks when he or she chooses and is not limited to set meal times, unless a documented modification applies.
A written instruction from a physician or other licensed practitioner giving the type of diet, texture, liquid consistency, restrictions and duration.
A documented change to a resident's HCBS settings right, supported by an assessed need, less intrusive methods tried, a time limit, regular review, and informed consent.

procedures: At admission and at least annually, the Home Manager and Delegating Nurse collect each resident's food allergies, intolerances, diagnoses affecting eating (such as diabetes, swallowing difficulty or GERD), food preferences, cultural and religious practices, and dislikes. They record these in the individual record under COMAR 10.22.02.13B (allergies and diagnoses) and in the IP.

Allergy information is posted in a place visible to staff but not in public view, and is placed on the resident's emergency ID and Medication Administration Record. Staff update all locations within 24 hours of any change.

Residents plan their own menus with staff support at least weekly, and are free to choose foods, seasonings, where they eat, and who they eat with. Staff offer healthy options, give information on nutrition without pressure, and respect choices that carry dignity of risk unless a documented health restriction exists.

Residents may get food and drink at any time, including between meals and overnight. The kitchen, refrigerator and pantry are open to residents. Food is not locked up, and snacks and beverages are always stocked and in reach, except where a documented modification applies.

A modification that limits access to food (for example, for Prader-Willi syndrome, pica, or a medical risk) may be proposed only by the resident's team. The team documents the specific assessed need, the positive interventions and less intrusive methods tried, how the modification will be used, a time limit and review schedule, informed consent (IR-06), and assurance that it causes no harm. It is not used for convenience, discipline or staff preference, and is reviewed through IR-02.

Diet orders are obtained from the physician or other licensed practitioner in writing. The Delegating Nurse reviews each order, confirms that it appears in the IP, and gives the Home Manager and staff written instructions, including texture, liquid consistency, portion, equipment, positioning, and supervision at meals.

Staff are trained on each resident's modified diet and meal-time supports before they work independently with that resident. The Home Manager confirms understanding through a return demonstration and signs the training record.
