policies.title: Volunteers, Contractors and Consultants
policies.applies_to: All volunteers, contracted staff, consultants and other care providers who work with or for individuals supported by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that anyone who is not a regular employee but who works with the individuals we support is screened, trained, supervised and bound by the same policies as employees.
policies.policy: Volunteers, consultants, contractors and other care providers must know and follow every policy in this manual, as COMAR 10.22.02.10 requires. The agency does not employ or contract with anyone whose criminal history indicates behavior potentially harmful to individuals, as COMAR 10.22.02.11 requires, and background screening applies to contractors and consultants as well as employees. Volunteers and care providers receive the same job training and the same DDA-approved training as staff, within the same time frames, before independent duties and within 3 months of starting, as COMAR 10.22.02.11 requires. No volunteer, contractor or consultant may have a conflict of interest with the agency or the individuals served. A volunteer or contractor is never counted toward the staffing plan unless fully screened and trained for that role, and is never left as the sole person responsible for individuals unless qualified to do so.

definitions.definition: An unpaid person who provides services or support to individuals at [AGENCY NAME]'s direction.
A person or business paid under an agreement to provide services, such as direct support, maintenance, transportation or therapy.
A professional engaged to advise the agency or the individuals, such as a nurse, behavior specialist or fiscal advisor.
A non-employee who provides direct care or support to an individual.

procedures: Before any volunteer, contractor or consultant begins, the Program Director completes an engagement form that states the role, the individuals involved, the expected duties and hours, and who supervises the person.

The agency obtains a written agreement or volunteer application for each person. It describes the role, confidentiality duties, mandatory reporting duties, and the requirement to follow all agency policies.

Criminal background and registry checks are completed before the person has any unsupervised access to individuals, using the process in ST-02. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews the results. A person whose history indicates potentially harmful behavior toward individuals is not engaged.

For a contractor that is a business, the agency obtains written confirmation that each of its workers assigned to the agency has passed an equivalent check. The agency keeps a list of the workers and the confirmation, and rechecks it on renewal of the contract.
Each person completes a conflict-of-interest disclosure (see GOV-10). [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews it before engagement. A person with a conflict that cannot be managed is not engaged.
Each person is given a copy or access to the policies relevant to their role and signs an acknowledgment that they know and will implement all policies. The acknowledgment is kept in their file.

Volunteers and contractors in direct support roles complete the job training, the DDA-approved training and the blood-borne pathogens training required for staff before independent duties, as set out in ST-03. They complete the remaining DDA-approved training and First Aid/CPR within 3 months of starting, as set out in ST-04.

A volunteer or direct-support contractor who has not completed required training works only under the direct, in-person supervision of a fully trained employee and is not counted in the staffing plan.
Volunteers and contractors who have contact with individuals meet the health and communicable disease requirements in ST-05 that apply to their role.

Volunteers and contractors do not administer medication, use restrictive interventions, handle individuals' funds, or assume the duties of paid staff unless they hold the required certification, training and written approval from [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

Volunteers and contractors receive information on abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting (see BH-04) and report any incident or concern to the Program Director immediately. They may also report directly to the Maryland Department of Health.

The Program Director supervises each volunteer, contractor and consultant on a schedule set in the engagement form. The Program Director records at least a quarterly review of the person's work and training status.
Consultants and contractors who see individuals' records are given access only to what they need and follow the privacy rules in IR-04.
The Program Director ends an engagement immediately if the person violates policy or is found to pose a risk to individuals. The reason is documented and reported to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] keeps a current roster of all volunteers, contractors and consultants with their screening and training status. This roster is reviewed at least quarterly and available to surveyors.

responsibilities.duty: Approves engagements, reviews background and conflict-of-interest results, and keeps the roster.
Defines roles, supervises non-employees, verifies training, and ensures they are not counted in staffing unless qualified.
Follow all agency policies, complete required training, protect confidentiality and report concerns.

documentation: Engagement forms and agreements
Background and registry check results, or contractor confirmations
Conflict-of-interest disclosures
Signed policy acknowledgments
Training records
Quarterly supervision notes
Roster of volunteers, contractors and consultants

policies.title: Individual Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All individual records kept by [AGENCY NAME] for people served at each licensed site; all staff who create, use or store them
policies.purpose: To keep a complete, accurate, accessible and secure record for each individual, to make medical information available in an emergency, and to retain records for the period COMAR 10.22.02.13 requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps each individual's record at the site where the person is served, as COMAR 10.22.02.13 requires. The record contains at least: application identifying information, emergency contact, next of kin, physician, diagnosis, allergies, medication list, the Individual Plan (IP), documentation of IP implementation, and anything else DDA requires. The agency makes the person's medical information readily accessible to emergency personnel. Records are kept for at least 6 years, even if the person no longer receives services or has died. Documents relevant to current services are kept for as long as the person is served, and records are organized for easy access. HIPAA documentation is kept for 6 years in line with 45 CFR 164.530(j).

definitions.definition: The set of documents, paper or electronic, that identifies an individual, describes their health and support needs, and documents the services provided.
The Individual Plan developed under COMAR 10.22.05 through person-centered planning.
The identifying and medical information emergency personnel need, such as diagnoses, allergies, medications, physician and emergency contacts.
The minimum time records must be kept: 6 years, counted from the date the person leaves services or dies, and longer if required by other law or DDA.

procedures: At admission (see PC-01), the Program Director opens a record at the site where the person lives and verifies that it contains application identifying information, emergency contact, next of kin, physician, diagnosis, allergies and current medication list.
The Program Director adds the IP within the time frames set in PC-02. Each revision of the IP is filed on the day it is finalized, and superseded versions are retained.
Staff document the implementation of the IP and daily supports as set out in PC-03, on the day the support is provided and before the end of the shift, and file the documentation in the record.

The Program Director adds other items DDA requires, such as authorizations, consents, rights restriction approvals, behavior plans, incident reports and health care documents. A record checklist is used to confirm that each is present.

A one-page emergency information sheet for each individual is kept in a designated, readily accessible location at the site and in the vehicle and updated whenever diagnoses, allergies, medications or contacts change. It is given to emergency personnel and travels with the individual to the hospital (see HW-04).
Records are kept in a locked cabinet or an access-controlled electronic system at the site. Only staff with a job-related need may view them. Access follows the privacy rules in IR-04 and RC-02.

Records are organized in a consistent order, by section, so that a staff member or surveyor can find any item within minutes. The Program Director reviews each record for completeness at least quarterly and records the result.

Entries are legible, dated, timed where relevant and signed or initialed with full name and title. Corrections are made by a single line through the entry, with date and initials. Entries are never obliterated or backdated.

An individual or proponent may review the record as permitted by IR-04. The Program Director logs each request and each release of information, including the date, recipient, purpose and what was released.

When a person leaves services or dies, the Program Director completes the record, notes the date of discharge or death, and has [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] approve it for archiving. The record is then moved to secure, organized storage and not discarded.

The agency retains each archived record for at least 6 years from the date the person left services or died. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] sets a destruction-eligible date on the file and keeps a log of archived records.

No record is destroyed while a complaint, investigation, audit, survey finding, legal hold or Medicaid review involving the person is open. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] must approve any destruction in writing.

Destruction of records that have passed the retention period is carried out by shredding or secure electronic deletion, and is recorded in the destruction log with date, method and the person who carried it out.

If the agency closes or a site is relocated, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] arranges for each record to be transferred with the person or secured for the remaining retention period, in coordination with DDA (see GOV-08 and PC-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures records are maintained, retained and destroyed in compliance with this policy and approves destruction.
Maintains a complete record at the site, performs quarterly reviews, and manages the emergency information sheet.
Document supports accurately and on time, and protect the confidentiality of records.

documentation: Individual record with required contents and completeness checklist
Emergency information sheet
Record release and access log
Archive and destruction log
Quarterly record review results

policies.title: Electronic Records, Backup and Security
policies.applies_to: All electronic systems that hold individual, staff or agency records, and all staff and contractors who use them
policies.purpose: To allow the use of electronic records while meeting COMAR 10.22.02.13, the HIPAA privacy and security rules, and the emergency plan requirement in COMAR 10.22.02.10 for off-site electronic backup.
policies.policy: Electronic records are permitted at [AGENCY NAME]. Under COMAR 10.22.02.13, electronic records must meet the same content, access and retention requirements as paper records, comply with the HIPAA privacy and security rules, and be properly backed up and stored off-site. Under COMAR 10.22.02.10, the agency's emergency plan provides for the backup and off-site electronic storage of appropriate records of individuals, staff and facility documents, and an electronic copy of the emergency plan is made available on request to emergency management organizations. The agency applies administrative, physical and technical safeguards and documents its security policies as required by 45 CFR 164.308, 164.312 and 164.316.

definitions.definition: Any individual, staff or agency record created, stored or transmitted in electronic form.
Protected health information in electronic form.
A copy of electronic records stored at a location or with a cloud service separate from the site where the records are created.
A documented review of threats and vulnerabilities to ePHI and the measures used to reduce them.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates a security official responsible for electronic records, and records the name in the security plan. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] approves before any new electronic records system is used.

Before adopting a system, the security official confirms in writing that it can meet the required record contents in RC-01, supports retention of at least 6 years, and can produce records quickly in an emergency. A business associate agreement is signed with any vendor that stores or handles ePHI.

The security official completes a documented security risk analysis before go-live, and repeats it at least annually and after any major system change or security incident. Identified risks are recorded with corrective actions and due dates.

Each user receives a unique login ID and strong password and, where the system allows, multi-factor authentication. Access is limited to what the person's job requires. Shared logins are not permitted.

The Program Director requests access for new staff, and the security official grants it. Access is removed the same day an employee, volunteer or contractor leaves or changes roles. Access is reviewed quarterly.

Workstations and devices that hold ePHI use automatic screen lock after inactivity, current security software and encryption. Devices are kept in a secure place, and a lost or stolen device is reported to the security official immediately.
Staff do not store ePHI on personal devices or personal email, and do not send ePHI by unencrypted email or text message. Approved secure methods are used for transmission.
The system keeps an audit log of who views, creates, changes or prints records. The security official reviews audit logs at least monthly for unusual access and investigates concerns.

Records are backed up automatically at least daily to an encrypted off-site location or cloud service covered by a business associate agreement. The backup includes records of individuals, staff and facility documents, as well as the emergency plan.

The security official verifies each month that backups completed, and tests restoration of a sample at least twice a year. Results and any problems are recorded, and failures are fixed within 5 business days.

An electronic copy of the emergency plan is kept off-site and is provided to local emergency management organizations on request. The Program Director ensures an up-to-date copy is available at each site (see HE-02).

The agency keeps a written contingency plan that covers data backup, emergency access to records, and operation during a system outage. During an outage, staff use paper downloads of the emergency information sheet and medication list so that care and emergency access are not interrupted.
Electronic signatures and entries identify the author, date and time, and cannot be changed without a visible audit trail. Corrected entries keep the original on file.

A suspected breach or unauthorized access is reported to the security official immediately. The security official investigates, contains the problem, and gives [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] a written assessment within 2 business days. The agency makes any individual, regulator or media notifications that HIPAA or DDA requires (see IR-04 and BH-05).

Electronic media that held ePHI is wiped or physically destroyed before disposal or reuse, and the disposal is recorded. All staff receive training on this policy at hire and annually, and the training is documented.

responsibilities.duty: Approves systems, designates the security official, and ensures resources for security and backup.
Manages access, risk analysis, audit log review, backups, restoration tests and breach response.
Requests and removes user access, ensures staff follow this policy, and maintains emergency paper contingencies.
Protect passwords and devices, use only approved methods, and report incidents immediately.

documentation: Security risk analyses and corrective action logs
Business associate agreements
User access requests and removal records
Audit log review records
Backup logs and restoration test results
Contingency plan
Breach investigation and notification records
Staff security training records

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], Program Director and all staff responsible for preparing or submitting reports and notices to DDA, OHCQ or the DDA regional office
policies.purpose: To provide one calendar of required reports, notices and submissions to the State, with the responsible person and the deadline for each, so that none is missed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes every report, notice and submission to DDA, OHCQ and the DDA regional office that is required by COMAR 10.22.02 and DDA procedures, on time and in the form required. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] maintains a compliance calendar of reporting deadlines and is accountable for it. The principal required reports are: incident reports to DDA under the DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII), within the time frames of the current policy as set out in BH-05; a plan of correction (POC) to OHCQ at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving findings; notice to the regional director of approval of a property-damage payment; notice to the DDA regional office when the emergency plan is activated; DDA approval of a revised Program Service Plan (PSP) before changes are implemented; DDA approval of the quality assurance (QA) plan and of substantive changes to it; 90 days' written notice to the Director before terminating services to an individual or surrendering the license; license renewal filed at least 60 days before expiration; and notice to DDA at least 30 days ahead of a site opening, closure or relocation.

definitions.definition: The DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, which sets what incidents must be reported to DDA and when.
Plan of correction: the agency's written response to findings from a survey or investigation, describing how and when each deficiency will be corrected.
Program Service Plan: the document describing each service the agency provides, its rationale, scope, staffing and training, and setting.
The Director of the Developmental Disabilities Administration, who issues, approves, conditions or denies licenses and approves terminations of services.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] keeps a compliance calendar listing every recurring and event-driven State report, its deadline, the responsible person and the date completed. It is reviewed at the monthly management meeting.

Incident reports: staff report any reportable incident to the Program Director immediately, and the Program Director submits the report to DDA within the time frames in the current PORII, using the current DDA reporting system, as set out in BH-05. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] checks the PORII for changes at least quarterly and updates BH-05 and staff training when it changes.

Plan of correction: when OHCQ issues findings after a licensure survey or complaint investigation, the Program Director and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] draft the POC. It is submitted at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving the findings, or sooner if OHCQ requires it. If more time is needed, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] requests an extension of up to 30 days from the OHCQ Director before the due date, in writing.

If OHCQ finds the POC unacceptable, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] resubmits a revised POC within 10 working days of notice. The agency then completes the corrective actions by the dates in the POC and keeps proof of each (see GOV-09).

Property-damage payment: when the agency approves a payment from an individual for property damage under IR-09, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reports the approval to the regional director in writing the same week and keeps a copy of the report and approval in the individual's record.

Emergency plan activation: when the emergency plan is activated for evacuation or shelter-in-place, the Program Director or the on-call manager notifies the DDA regional office as soon as it is safe to do so. The notice is documented with time, person notified and the situation (see HE-02).

PSP: before any change to a service, scope, staffing, training, setting, location or number of individuals served, the Program Director drafts a revised PSP and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits it to DDA. The change is not implemented until DDA approves it. The governing body also reviews and updates the PSP at least every 3 years (see GOV-07).
QA plan: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits the QA plan and any substantive change to DDA for approval before the change takes effect, and files the approval in the QA file (see GOV-04).

License renewal: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] files the renewal application at least 60 days before the license expires, with all required attachments. The expiration date is on the compliance calendar with a reminder at 120 and 90 days (see GOV-02).

Termination of services: the agency may terminate services to an individual only for good cause with the Director's written approval. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] gives the Director 90 days' written notice, gives the individual and proponent written notice of the right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16, and copies the regional office and the team (see PC-05). The agency also tracks days of continuous absence. Services are considered terminated after 60 consecutive days of absence unless the Director decides otherwise, so [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] notifies the regional office at 45 days of absence to request direction.

Voluntary surrender of the license: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits a closure schedule to the Director at least 90 days before the proposed surrender and obtains the Director's approval before closing (see GOV-08).
Site opening, closure or relocation: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] notifies DDA in writing at least 30 days before any site opens, closes or relocates, and the notice is filed with the site file (see GOV-08).

Other DDA-required reports: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews DDA bulletins and provider communications at least monthly. Any newly required report is added to the compliance calendar and assigned to a responsible person within 5 business days.
